**01 · Sign Up** — split layout: navy brand panel ("Sell it to someone who gets it") with three trust bullets, and a form card capturing Columbia email, username, phone, nationality, college/school, grade (Undergrad/Grad/Faculty), ZIP. Footer credits `ENGI 4503 · Analytics in Python · Brian · Jae · Vinayak · Kobe`.

**02 · Sign In** — passwordless magic-link only ("Email me a sign-in link", 15-min expiry), plus a 3-step explainer of email verification and a mockup of the actual verification email.

**03 · Feed / Search** — the core screen. Left filter rail with a "Trust filters" block (Same ZIP / Same nationality / Same college toggles), category checkboxes with counts, price range + slider, condition, a **distance-from-ZIP** slider (0.5–10 mi), nationality and school dropdowns. Right side: "612 items within 2.5 miles of 10027", removable filter chips, and a 4-up card grid. Cards carry condition badges, price, `ZIP · distance · time ago`, and match badges (`SAME ZIP`, `SAME COUNTRY`, `SAME SCHOOL`). Two cards are marked `EXTERNAL` with eBay / Facebook Marketplace sources.

**04 · Item Detail** — gallery with 5 thumbnails, sticky right column with price, category/condition/pickup/posted table, Email seller / Text seller / Save / Share. Seller card shows verified handle, school + nationality, the shared match badges with the line "You share all three with this seller — that is why this listing sits at the top of your feed," plus items-sold / avg-reply / member-since stats. Safety callout for on-campus handover, then "More from @brian_dw".

**05 · Upload Item** — two-column form (photos w/ cover, title, category chips, condition, price + free/negotiable, pickup ZIP, description) with a **live preview** card on the right that renders the feed card as you type, and a note that badges are automatic and the audience is set by each buyer's filters.

**Design system read:** navy `#1E3A6E`-ish primary on near-white `#F7F9FC`, white cards with soft borders and ~12–16px radii, pill chips/badges, pastel gradient placeholders standing in for photos, system sans throughout.

```
# Marketplace

A marketplace where you choose who you trade with — filtered by the things you
already have in common.

**Team:** Brian (Dongwoo), Jaewon (Jae), Vinayak, Kobe

## The Problem

Columbia students buy and sell constantly: furniture at move-out, appliances,
textbooks, winter coats. Today that happens in group chats, where a listing
scrolls away within an hour and can never be searched, or on Facebook
Marketplace, where you are meeting a stranger with no accountability and
haggling in norms you may not share. Neither gives you a way to find the people
you would actually be comfortable trading with.

## Who It's For

Columbia students, verified by a `@columbia.edu` email address. Nobody without
one can sign in during the pilot. Our sharpest use case is MBA students, who
arrive and leave on a fixed two-year cycle, furnish an apartment from scratch,
and liquidate it on the way out.

**The demand is already proven.** The Korean Columbia Association group chat has
roughly 1,000 members, and the overwhelming majority of its traffic is people
buying and selling from each other — a marketplace that exists today with no
infrastructure, running entirely on messages that scroll away within the hour.

That community is not our market. It is our proof that the need is real, and our
route to a populated launch. We plan to recruit KCA members as our first sellers
and have them post the items they are already trying to sell in the chat, so the
platform opens with genuine listings from verified Columbia students instead of
an empty page. Once that flywheel is turning, the same mechanism extends to every
other circle a Columbia student belongs to.

## How We Solve It

A marketplace where every user declares four attributes — **location,
nationality, school, industry** — and every listing carries the same four from
its seller. Buyers turn those attributes on as filters, so the same pool of
listings becomes a different marketplace depending on who you are and what you
care about.

The bet: trust in a used-goods trade comes from accountability, not from star
ratings. When a seller shares your school and your country, a bad transaction
has social consequences and you both already know how the exchange is supposed
to go. Karrot (당근마켓) built Korea's largest marketplace on GPS-verified
neighborhoods; we are testing whether affiliation does the same job in the US.

## Key Features

   verified by e
```

```
import pandas as pd
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest, proportion_confint
engine = create_engine(READONLY_DATABASE_URL)
# every feed impression, flat: one row per listing shown
imp = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT e.session_id,
           (i.item->>'id')::uuid            AS listing_id,
           (i.item->>'badges_shown')::bool  AS treated
    FROM events e,
         LATERAL jsonb_array_elements(e.payload->'listing_ids') AS i(item)
    WHERE e.event_type = 'feed_view'
""", engine)
contacts = pd.read_sql(
    "SELECT session_id, listing_id FROM events WHERE event_type='contact_click'",
    engine)
# did this exact impression turn into a contact in the same session?
imp["contacted"] = imp.merge(contacts, how="left", indicator=True,
                             on=["session_id", "listing_id"])["_merge"].eq("both")
g = imp.groupby("treated")["contacted"].agg(["sum", "count"])
z, p = proportions_ztest(g["sum"], g["count"])
```

**Claude:**

**Plan is up:** https://claude.ai/code/artifact/eb711236-6f96-4c6b-9502-98db36f714cb — shareable with Brian, Jae and Vinayak.

**What I did to get there:** the Figma MCP is rate-limited on your View seat, so I read the file through Chrome instead. All five pages. The important find is that **04 · User Flow** is the closest thing to a written spec — every flow card carries an `INPUTS` / `RULE` / `DEFAULT` line — and **06 · Account Settings** (a sixth desktop screen the MCP metadata didn't list) is the only place the whole user record appears at once. That's where the model comes from.

**The core of the plan:**

- **Every column, sourced.** 12 user columns and 15 listing columns, each one traced to the screen that proves it exists, with its generation rule. Seven declared user fields plus five derived ones (`items_sold`, `avg_reply_min`, `member_since`…) that must be *computed*, not drawn — Item Detail shows "14 items sold" right above the seller's actual grid.
- **The mockup is the acceptance test.** The Feed screen's numbers are mutually consistent for one specific viewer (Brian Lee, 10027, South Korea, CBS, Graduate). So the target isn't "looks plausible" — it's: seed the data, run the feed query as him, get back 612 within 2.5 mi, 412 same-ZIP, 188 same-nationality, 254 same-college, and the six category counts. That fixes the volume at ~450 users / ~1,220 active listings.
- **The couplings a naive generator breaks** — names agreeing with nationality, grade legal for college, description never contradicting condition, sold items being old items, counters as one funnel — plus 14 invariants a `validate.py` enforces.
- **Ten rows that exist to break screens**, taken from the Screen States page: the phone-less seller, the one-photo gallery, the $0 listing, the filter combo that returns zero.

**Three things I'd want answered before I generate 450 rows:**

1. **The college list.** "Business (CBS)" is the only value anywhere in the file, and every filter depends on exact matching. I've proposed the 13-school list — someone should confirm it.
2. **Are the eBay / Facebook Marketplace listings mine?** They're a different row shape — no seller, no badges, a link out. Easy to add, but not if Vinayak's scraping already produces them.
3. **Grade.** It's a required signup field and an Account Settings dropdown, but it's never a filter or a badge. That's the same thing Jaewon's comment on Screen States is asking about.

Two things I noticed that are probably design bugs rather than data decisions: the feed shows ZIP 10024 at both 1.2 mi and 1.6 mi, which can't both be true under the "distance is measured between ZIP centroids" rule the Item Detail page states; and the sidebar category counts sum to 1,219 while the condition counts on the same screen sum to 743, so the two facet groups are being counted against different filter contexts. Both are in the doc as questions 7 and 8.

I haven't written any code — say the word and I'll start at step 1.

```
A secondhand marketplace restricted to Columbia students, verified by

sorted by proximity, with a strong trust signal attached to every seller. Karrot
uses GPS-verified neighbourhoods; we use **ZIP code + distance in miles**, plus
three affiliation attributes.
```

```
Desktop is two columns: gallery + description + safety note on the left (700px),
a sticky action panel on the right (420px). Mobile is a full-bleed photo with
floating back/share, then content, then a fixed bottom action bar.

Right panel order: status pill · title · price · attribute table
(Category / Condition / Pickup / Posted) · **contact buttons (§5.1)** ·
Save + Share · the phone-disclosure line · seller card · "more from this seller".

The seller card is where overlap-only disclosure becomes visible, and it is worth
being pedantic about: **the item, the price and the photos are identical for every
viewer; only the seller block changes.** That is what makes the internal-vs-external
engagement comparison a clean experiment — the difference cannot come from the item.

Listing statuses render differently: `active` (green pill, contact enabled),
`reserved` (amber, still visible in the feed, "join the queue"), `sold`
(struck-through price, dimmed, contact locked, drops out of search but the page
stays reachable).
```

**Claude:**

Pulled `6fa0597` (2 commits: `docs/UX_SPEC.md` + 19 screen PNGs). Plan is reconciled and republished at the same link — https://claude.ai/code/artifact/eb711236-6f96-4c6b-9502-98db36f714cb

**Scorecard: 21 confirmed, 4 corrected, 6 columns I'd missed, 1 real conflict.**

**Where I was wrong:**

1. **Facet counts are conditional.** §5.4 says every count next to a filter is "the count *if you applied it*, evaluated against all other active filters." So my inference that the six category counts sum to the total pool (1,219) is void — that was the foundation of my calibration idea.
2. **`listing_status` is `draft | active | reserved | sold`.** No `delisted`; `reserved` is a real state with its own amber rendering (`D4`). I'd have generated zero rows for a screen that exists.
3. **Don't plant the effect.** §9: generate both tiers "with the same base rates and let the analysis find (or fail to find) the effect." My v1 said to plant an in-group discount and badge lift and document them. Reversed. The spec draws a sharp line — the 3× seasonality spike *is* to be planted, because it's scenery; the tier difference is not, because it's the finding.
4. **Username charset** is `[a-zA-Z0-9._]` — dots and uppercase legal. My regex was too narrow.

**Columns I missed entirely:** `listings.subcategory` (furniture is two-level — the "Furniture › Desks" breadcrumb was right there), `users.display_name`, `users.is_verified`, `users.status`, `updated_at`, and `karrot` as a third external source. Plus the big one — **four event tables**, not three counters on the listing. The counters are denormalised summaries of them.

**The conflict, which is Brian's to resolve:** §9 proposes ~1,000 members and ~1,500 listings. The Feed screen shows 612 results with six filters active. Taking only three of those filters, priced from §9's own distributions — category 0.50 × condition 0.75 × price ≈0.45 — gives a 16.9% survival rate. That's 253 items from the whole corpus, and 612 survivors would need ~3,627 listings *inside the 2.5-mile radius alone*, before distance or the trust toggles apply. The two can't both stand. My vote is redrawing the mockup's counts, since 10,000+ listings from 1,000 members isn't a plausible pilot either.

**What the spec answered:** the school list (14 values — my guess missed the SEAS undergrad/grad split and `vps`), the Korean share (10%), the external tier being mine, and the 10024 distance — §4.6 fixes it at 1.6 mi, so the mockup's 1.2 was an artefact, as were three other card distances.

**Two new things worth your attention before I build:**

- **§10 puts the event pipelines on data/analysis** — i.e. probably you, not just "users and listings." That roughly doubles the job, and `filter_events.result_count` is the hard part since it has to match what the feed query would really have returned. Confirm with Brian.
- **Two ZIPs are doing two different jobs.** §5.2 computes distance from `listing.zip_code`; §5.3 computes the SAME ZIP badge from `seller.zip_code`. A listing can therefore show a SAME ZIP badge while displaying 3 miles. Probably unintended.

Also: `LionsListBuildSpec.pdf` is now orphaned — the new README doesn't reference it, and it contradicts UX_SPEC. Might be worth deleting so nobody reads it by accident.

````bash
tokens = set(re.findall(r"\b[a-z][a-z_]{2,}\b", block))
enum_names = {"category", "subcategory", "condition", "grade",
              "listing_status", "source", "school"}
prose = {"other", "categories", "are", "single", "level", "for", "now", "labels",
         "grouped", "in", "the", "ui", "as", "undergraduate", "and",
         "professional", "used", "new", "like", "fair", "good"}
spec_values = tokens - enum_names - prose

mine = set()
for group in (V.CATEGORIES, V.CONDITIONS, V.GRADES, V.SCHOOLS,
              V.LISTING_STATUSES, V.SOURCES):
    mine |= set(group)
for subs in V.SUBCATEGORIES.values():
    mine |= set(subs)

missing = sorted(v for v in spec_values if v not in mine)
invented = sorted(v for v in mine if v not in block)

print("values in §4.5 not in the module :", missing or "none")
print("values in the module not in §4.5 :", invented or "none")
print()
print("counts — categories %d, subcategories %d, conditions %d, grades %d,"
      % (len(V.CATEGORIES), sum(len(s) for s in V.SUBCATEGORIES.values()),
         len(V.CONDITIONS), len(V.GRADES)))
print("         schools %d, statuses %d, sources %d"
      % (len(V.SCHOOLS), len(V.LISTING_STATUSES), len(V.SOURCES)))
print()
print("grade x school constraint:")
for s in ("columbia_college", "cbs", "seas_undergrad", "seas_grad"):
    print("   %-18s -> %s" % (s, ", ".join(V.grades_for_school(s))))
print()
print("subcategory guard:", 
      V.is_valid_subcategory("furniture", "desks"),
      V.is_valid_subcategory("textbooks", "desks"),
      V.is_valid_subcategory("textbooks", None))
PY
````

**Step 1 done.** Two files on `feat/seed-data`:

- `seed/__init__.py`
- `seed/vocabularies.py` — [seed/vocabularies.py:1](seed/vocabularies.py)

**What's in it:** all seven §4.5 vocabularies transcribed verbatim in the spec's own order (8 categories, 5 furniture subcategories, 4 conditions, 3 grades, 14 schools, 4 listing statuses, 4 sources), plus the four smaller enums the spec names elsewhere rather than in §4.5 — `user_status` (§4.1), `view_surface` and `enquiry_channel` (§4.4), and the five sort options (§5.4). Standard library only, so the generator, the validator and eventually the API can all import it.

**Verified rather than assumed.** I diffed the module against the §4.5 code block in `UX_SPEC.md` directly: zero values in the spec that aren't in the module, zero in the module that aren't in the spec. Import-time self-checks also assert the internal consistency that actually breaks in practice — labels covering every value and nothing more, `SCHOOL_GROUPS` partitioning `SCHOOLS` exactly, no subcategory claimed by two categories.

**Three judgment calls I made, all reversible:**

1. **Display labels are marked PROVISIONAL** where the spec doesn't fix them. Only a few are evidenced — the four condition labels are written out in §4.5 (with an em dash: `Used — good`), `Business (CBS)` is on two screens, and `eBay` / `Facebook Marketplace` are on the feed cards. I inferred the other eleven school labels in that same parenthetical style. Worth a glance from Brian before they reach a screen; the *values* are what everything depends on and those are exact.
2. **`grades_for_school()` encodes the constraint the spec implies but never states** — undergraduate only at the three undergraduate schools, graduate only at the eleven others, faculty/staff legal everywhere. The `seas_undergrad` / `seas_grad` split is the spec quietly acknowledging this; nothing else would explain listing SEAS twice.
3. **I folded the field constraints in** — the email and username regexes, title 60 / description 1000, 10 photos, radius presets, badge attributes. Not vocabularies strictly, but the validator and the generator both need them and two copies would eventually disagree.

Also included `postgres_enum_ddl()`, which emits the `CREATE TYPE` statements from the same tuples — so when step 8 writes `seed.sql`, the DDL can't drift from what the generator produced.

Nothing committed yet. Ready for step 2 (the ZIP centroid table) when you want it.

```
UX_SPEC §9 fixes the four largest shares -- "US ~35%, China ~18%, South Korea

us.
```

```
"""Item templates, price bands and description fragments.

This is the slow part of the generator and the part that decides whether the feed
reads as a real marketplace or as filler. UX_SPEC §9 fixes the category mix, the
condition skew and four of the eight price ranges; everything else here is ours.

Three rules the templates encode, none of which fall out of independent draws:

* **A title is a category's title.** Each template belongs to exactly one
  category (and, for furniture, one subcategory), so a textbook never gets a
  colour slot and a desk never gets an edition number.
* **Price follows the item, then the condition.** Each template carries its own
  band for a ``used_good`` example -- a used MALM desk is not priced from the same
  distribution as a used Aeron chair -- and the condition multiplier is applied on
  top, then clamped back into the category range from §9.
* **A description cannot contradict its condition.** The opening line is drawn
  from a pool keyed on condition, so a ``new`` item never mentions a scuff. This
  is the coupling that most obviously breaks in generated data.

Slot values are drawn from :data:`SLOTS`; a template may name any slot in it.
"""
```

> _old_string_

```
def _fill(rng, template: str) -> str:
    """Resolve every ``{slot}`` in a template from :data:`SLOTS`."""
    out = template
    while "{" in out:
        start = out.index("{")
        end = out.index("}", start)
        slot = out[start + 1:end]
        out = out[:start] + rng.choice(SLOTS[slot]) + out[end + 1:]
    return out
```

> _new_string_

```
def _fill(rng, template: str) -> str:
    """Resolve every ``{slot}`` in a template from :data:`SLOTS`."""
    out = template
    while "{" in out:
        start = out.index("{")
        end = out.index("}", start)
        slot = out[start + 1:end]
        out = out[:start] + rng.choice(SLOTS[slot]) + out[end + 1:]
    return out


def _sentence_case(text: str) -> str:
    """Capitalise the first letter only.

    Templates that open with a slot ("{cookware}", "{outerwear}, {clothing_size}")
    otherwise produce "cast iron skillet" as a title. Brand casing further along
    the string is left alone -- "IKEA MALM" and 'Dell 24"' must survive.
    """
    return text[:1].upper() + text[1:] if text else text
```

```
"""Listing and photo generation (UX_SPEC §4.2/§4.3, distributions from §9).

**Sellers are Zipf-shaped, not uniform.** §6.4 puts a "more from this seller" rail
on the item detail page, which only means anything if some people are liquidating
a whole apartment while most post once. Roughly half of all sellers post a single
item; the top few percent hold a quarter of the inventory.

**Sold-ness is derived from time, not assigned.** Drawing ``status`` directly
would produce listings posted twelve minutes ago and already sold. Instead each
internal listing gets a *will it ever sell* coin flip and a days-to-sale draw, and
becomes ``sold`` only if that date has already passed. Recent listings are
therefore mostly still active for the same reason they are in real life, and the
days-to-sale figures the analysis computes are honestly right-censored.

**Pickup ZIP equals the seller's ZIP.** §5.2 measures distance from
``listings.zip_code`` while §5.3 computes the SAME ZIP badge from
```

```
"""A local reimplementation of the §5.3-§5.5 feed rules.

The generator needs this for one reason: ``filter_events.result_count`` (§4.4) is

analysis is measuring my noise rather than the product. So the count logged
against every simulated toggle is the count this query actually returns.

It is deliberately a *separate* implementation from whatever the API ends up
doing, so the two can be compared. If ``GET /filters/counts`` and this disagree,
one of them has a bug -- that is a feature of having both.

Three rules from the spec are implemented here:

* **§5.3 badges** -- computed per ``(viewer, listing)`` pair, never stored. An
  attribute that does not match is absent, not false.
* **§5.4 filters** -- and specifically the honesty rule: "every count shown next
  to a filter is the count *if you applied it*, evaluated against all other
  active filters". So facet counts are conditional, not absolute.
* **§5.5 two-tier** -- external listings have no seller, therefore no badges, and
  the three trust filters exclude them entirely.

        current = {slot: getattr(self, slot) for slot in self.__slots__}
```

```
"""The four event tables (UX_SPEC §4.4), and the counter backfill.

§9 fixes the funnel: "views >> saves >> enquiries (roughly 100 : 8 : 1)". The
important structural decision is that these are generated *as one funnel* -- a
save is drawn from a view that happened, an enquiry from a save-eligible view --
rather than as three independent per-listing numbers. That is what lets
``listings.view_count`` and friends be a true ``COUNT(*)`` over these tables
instead of three decorative integers that disagree with them.

Two couplings the spec forces:

* **§5.1** -- an ``sms`` enquiry is only possible when the seller supplied a phone
  *and* left texting enabled. Email is always available and "can never be turned
  off", so every other enquiry is email.
* **§5.5** -- external listings have no seller, so they collect views and saves
  but can never produce an enquiry; the contact button links out instead.

The one thing §9 explicitly forbids is planting the finding: "do not hard-code a
difference -- generate both tiers with the same base rates and let the analysis
find (or fail to find) the effect". So the view model below reads only from
listing age, photo count and price. It never looks at ``source``, and it never
looks at whether a badge would be shown.

    return next(reversed(list(weights)))
```

```
"""Rows that exist so a screen state can be demoed.

UX_SPEC §7 gives every interaction state an ID, and §10 says "a screen is not done
until its states render". A state with no matching row cannot be built against, and
random draws do not reliably produce the awkward ones -- a 10-photo listing, a
seller who shares nothing with the viewer, a filter combination that returns zero.

§9 makes the same argument for the one case it cares about: "leave ~30% of phone
NULL -- the email-only contact layout must be exercised by the data, not just by a
design state."

So this module runs after generation and before events, mutates a small number of
rows to guarantee each state, and returns a manifest naming the row that covers
each one. Nothing is appended, so the corpus size stays exactly what was asked for.

It also installs **the reference member**: the user the Figma mockups are drawn
for (``@brian_dw``, 10027, South Korea, CBS, graduate). Having a fixed identity to
sign in as makes every screenshot reproducible.
"""

    for row in rows:
        if predicate(row):

    return default
```

```
"""Invariants the generated corpus must satisfy.

These are not tests of the generator's taste -- they are the constraints a backend
would enforce with NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE and foreign keys, plus the handful that
UX_SPEC states in prose and no column type can express (§5.1's phone/text
coupling, §4.2's is_free/price equivalence, §4.4's counters being summaries).

Anything that fails here would either fail to load into Postgres or would render a
screen that contradicts itself. Run it after every regeneration; it is cheap.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re

from . import vocabularies as V
from . import zips as Z


class Failure:
    __slots__ = ("rule", "detail", "sample")

    def __init__(self, rule, detail, sample=None):
        self.rule = rule
        self.detail = detail
        self.sample = sample
```

```
"""Write the corpus to ``data/`` as CSV and as a loadable ``seed.sql``.

CSV is the interchange format because it loads into Postgres with ``\\copy``, into
pandas with one call, and into a spreadsheet when somebody wants to eyeball it.
``seed.sql`` exists so the backend can bring a database up without running Python.

Conventions, chosen once so the loader does not have to guess:

* timestamps are ISO-8601 with a ``+00:00`` offset (the columns are ``timestamptz``)
* booleans are ``true`` / ``false``
* NULL is the empty field, which is what ``\\copy ... WITH (FORMAT csv, NULL '')``
  expects
* the header row uses the exact column names from UX_SPEC §4
"""

    "default_filter_same_school", "is_verified", "status",
    "created_at", "updated_at",
)

LISTING_COLUMNS = (

SAVE_COLUMNS = ("id", "listing_id", "user_id", "created_at")
ENQUIRY_COLUMNS = ("id", "listing_id", "buyer_id", "channel", "created_at")
FILTER_EVENT_COLUMNS = ("id", "user_id", "filter_key", "value", "result_count", "created_at")

ZIP_COLUMNS = ("zip_code", "neighbourhood", "borough", "lat", "lon", "miles_from_campus")


def _render(value):
    if value is None:
        return ""
    if isinstance(value, bool):
        return "true" if value else "false"
    if isinstance(value, dt.datetime):
        return value.replace(microsecond=0).isoformat() + "+00:00"
    return value


def write_csv(path, columns, rows):
    with open(path, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        writer = csv.writer(handle, quoting=csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL)
        writer.writerow(columns)
        for row in rows:
            writer.writerow([_render(row[c]) for c in columns])
    return len(rows)
```

```
    python -m seed.generate                       # defaults from UX_SPEC §9
    python -m seed.generate --users 2000 --listings 3000

Deterministic: the same ``--seed`` with the same counts produces byte-identical

Order matters and is not arbitrary:

Edge cases run *before* events because they change listing statuses and seller
```

**Claude:**

One genuine finding from the validator: I'd written that invariant wrong. Saves and enquiries are independent per view, so a listing can have an enquiry and no saves — someone emails without saving. The ordering is an aggregate property, not a per-row one.


> **`Edit`**

> `/Users/kobeko/Desktop/MBA:MS/Python_bootcamp/secondhand_marketplace/seed/validate.py`

> _old_string_

```
    offenders = [l for l in listings
                 if not (l["view_count"] >= l["save_count"] >= l["enquiry_count"])]
    if offenders:
        fail("13 views >= saves >= enquiries", "%d listings" % len(offenders))
```

> _new_string_

```
    # Per listing, both saves and enquiries are drawn from views, so each is
    # bounded by the view count. They are NOT ordered against each other: a
    # buyer can email about an item without saving it first, so a listing with
    # one enquiry and no saves is correct, not a bug.
    offenders = [l for l in listings
                 if l["save_count"] > l["view_count"]
                 or l["enquiry_count"] > l["view_count"]]
    if offenders:
        fail("13 saves/enquiries <= views", "%d listings" % len(offenders),
             "%s: v=%d s=%d e=%d" % (offenders[0]["id"][:8], offenders[0]["view_count"],
                                     offenders[0]["save_count"],
                                     offenders[0]["enquiry_count"]))
    # The 100 : 8 : 1 ordering from §9 is an aggregate property.
    totals = (sum(l["view_count"] for l in listings),
              sum(l["save_count"] for l in listings),
              sum(l["enquiry_count"] for l in listings))
    if not totals[0] >= totals[1] >= totals[2]:
        fail("13 funnel ordering in aggregate", "views/saves/enquiries = %s" % (totals,))
```

> _new_string_

```
    # C4 -- an empty feed has to be reachable from filters a person would
    # plausibly set. Searched rather than hard-coded, because what is empty
    # depends on the corpus size: a probe that returns nothing at 300 listings
    # returns one or two at 1,500.
    probes = (
        FilterState(radius_mi=0.5, same_school=True, same_nationality=True,
                    categories=["sports"], price_max_cents=2000),
        FilterState(radius_mi=0.5, same_school=True, same_nationality=True,
                    categories=["free_stuff"], conditions=["new"]),
        FilterState(radius_mi=0.5, same_zip=True, same_school=True,
                    same_nationality=True, categories=["bikes_transport"],
                    conditions=["new"]),
        FilterState(radius_mi=0.5, same_zip=True, same_school=True,
                    same_nationality=True, categories=["sports"],
                    conditions=["new", "used_fair"], price_max_cents=1500),
    )
    empty_probe = None
    tried = []
    for probe in probes:
        count = feed.count(reference, probe)
        tried.append(count)
        if count == 0:
            empty_probe = probe
            break
    findings.append((
        "C4_empty_state",
        empty_probe is not None,
        ("%s -> 0 results" % empty_probe.describe()) if empty_probe
        else "no probe emptied the feed; counts were %s" % tried,
    ))

    return findings
```

```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Regenerate the placeholder photos referenced by ``listing_photos.url``.

The images are *not* committed -- there are ~5,800 of them and they carry no
information. This script rebuilds them from the CSV, deterministically, so two
people running it get the same pictures.

    python3 scripts/make_photos.py                 # into ./photos
    python3 scripts/make_photos.py --out web/public/photos

Each photo is a soft vertical gradient in one of the ``01 · Foundations`` brand
tints, chosen from a hash of the listing id so a listing's photos are a coherent
set and the same listing always gets the same colour. The category name is drawn
in the corner the way the mockup's placeholder cards do.

Pillow is used when available (it produces the WebP the URLs name). Without it,
the script writes SVGs alongside and prints how to point at them instead -- the
generator does not depend on this running at all.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import csv
import hashlib
import os
import sys

# The pastel card fills from docs/screens/91-foundations.png, as (top, bottom).
GRADIENTS = (
    ((0xC7, 0xD9, 0xF0), (0xA8, 0xC2, 0xE4)),   # brand blue
    ((0xE8, 0xD6, 0xB8), (0xD8, 0xBE, 0x92)),   # sand
    ((0xD5, 0xD8, 0xE6), (0xB9, 0xBF, 0xD4)),   # slate
    ((0xC9, 0xE0, 0xCE), (0xA6, 0xC9, 0xB0)),   # sage
    ((0xEE, 0xD2, 0xD2), (0xDE, 0xB0, 0xB0)),   # blush
    ((0xDC, 0xD2, 0xEA), (0xC0, 0xB0, 0xDC)),   # lilac
    ((0xDD, 0xDD, 0xDD), (0xBB, 0xBB, 0xBB)),   # neutral
)

WIDTH, HEIGHT = 800, 600


def _palette_for(listing_id: str, position: int):
    digest = hashlib.sha256(listing_id.encode()).digest()
    base = digest[0] % len(GRADIENTS)
    # Later photos of the same listing shift one step, so a gallery looks like a
    # set of shots rather than seven copies of one image.
    return GRADIENTS[(base + position) % len(GRADIENTS)]


def _write_svg(path, top, bottom, label):
    svg = (
        '<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="%d" height="%d">'
        '<defs><linearGradient id="g" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">'
        '<stop offset="0%%" stop-color="rgb(%d,%d,%d)"/>'
        '<stop offset="100%%" stop-color="rgb(%d,%d,%d)"/>'
        '</linearGradient></defs>'
        '<rect width="100%%" height="100%%" fill="url(#g)"/>'
        '<text x="28" y="%d" font-family="Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif" '
        'font-size="20" letter-spacing="2" fill="rgba(20,32,52,0.55)">%s</text>'
        '</svg>'
    ) % (WIDTH,
… [2,654 more characters]
```

````
# Mock data — implementation spec

**Owner:** Kobe · **Branch:** `feat/seed-data` · **Generator:** `seed/` · **Output:** `data/`

**Source of truth:** [`docs/UX_SPEC.md`](UX_SPEC.md). Every column, enum value and
distribution below is traceable to a section of it, and every section reference in
this document is a real one you can go and check. Where UX_SPEC is silent I have
made a choice and said so; where UX_SPEC and the Figma disagree, UX_SPEC wins.

> **If you are building the backend, read §5, §6 and §7.** §5 is the column-by-column
> reference. §6 is the logic that is deliberately *not* in the data and which the API
> has to compute. §7 is the list of constraints your DDL should enforce — the
> generator already guarantees all of them, so any violation you see later came from
> application code, not from the seed.

---

## 1. What this is

A deterministic generator that produces a full working corpus for Columbia Market:
1,000 members, 1,500 listings, their photos, and the four event tables from
UX_SPEC §4.4. It exists so the feed, the item page and the analysis notebook all
have something real to run against before a single member signs up.

It is not a fixture file. It is a program with the spec's distributions written
into it, so the corpus can be regenerated at any size, and so every number in it
can be traced to a rule rather than to a typo.

**Scope decision:** the four event tables are included. UX_SPEC §10 puts the §9
generator *and* the `filter_events` / `enquiries` pipelines on data/analysis, and
`listings.view_count` and friends are summaries of those tables — generating the
counters without the events would guarantee they disagree with whatever anyone
produced later.

---

## 2. Running it

```bash
python3 -m seed.generate                            # §9 defaults, writes data/
python3 -m seed.generate --users 5000 --listings 8000
python3 -m seed.generate --seed 42 --out /tmp/out
python3 -m seed.generate --no-export                # report + validate only
```

No third-party dependencies. Standard library only, Python 3.9+. A full run takes
````

```
        # Pareto tail: most people post once or twice, a few liquidate a flat.
```

**Claude:**

All eight steps are done, on `feat/seed-data`. Nothing committed — the working tree is yours to review.

## What runs

```
python3 -m seed.generate        # ~1 second, no dependencies, Python 3.9+
```

Verified deterministic: two consecutive runs produce identical MD5s for every CSV.

## What it produced

1,000 members · 1,500 listings (1,350 internal + 150 external) · 5,849 photos · 72,602 views · 6,370 saves · 742 enquiries · 3,197 filter events. **All 16 invariant groups pass.** 26 MB in `data/`.

Realised distributions land within a couple of points of UX_SPEC §9 everywhere — nationality 35.6/18.1/8.9/8.0 against 35/18/10/8, condition 46.0/28.7 against 45/30, phone NULL 31.1% against ~30%, funnel 100 : 8.8 : 1 against 100 : 8 : 1, and the May/August spike at 178 and 332 against a 32 trough.

## The document

`docs/mock_data_spec.md` is written for whoever builds the backend. Its three load-bearing sections:

- **§5 — every column**, with type, nullability and how the value is produced.
- **§6 — the logic that is deliberately not in the data.** Distance, badges, and the one that's easy to get silently wrong: §5.4's facet counts are *conditional* ("the count if you applied it, evaluated against all other active filters"), not `GROUP BY category`. `seed/feed.py` is a reference implementation to compare against — if it and `GET /filters/counts` disagree, one of them has a bug.
- **§7 — 16 constraints for the DDL.** The generator already guarantees all of them, so a later violation came from application code, not the seed.

## Four things worth your attention

**The validator caught a bug in my own thinking.** I'd written `views >= saves >= enquiries` as a per-row invariant. It fails, correctly — saves and enquiries are independent draws from views, so a listing with one enquiry and no saves is a buyer emailing without saving. The ordering is an aggregate property and is now checked as one.

**§4.6's distances aren't all great-circle.** `python3 -m seed.zips` audits them: five of eight agree within 0.3 mi, three don't. Astoria is the tell — 3.6 mi in a straight line, but §4.6 says 5.2, which is what you get crossing the East River. The §4.6 figures look like *travel* distance while §5.2 specifies haversine. I kept §4.6 verbatim as sign-up display copy and compute feed distances from centroids, but the design should pick one.

**"4 min average reply" is not in the dataset.** Nothing in §4 records a reply and in-app chat is out of scope, so it can't be derived from anything we store. Either the seller card drops it or `users` gets a column we all agree is decorative.

**Nothing is planted except scenery.** Per §9's explicit instruction, the view model reads only listing age, photo count and price — never `source`, never whether a badge would show. So the badge experiment will find nothing on this data, which is the correct outcome, and §9 of the doc says so in bold. Seasonality and the category/price mixes *are* planted, and they're listed.

Two open items I flagged rather than decided: whether deactivated members' listings stay in the feed (§5.4 has no `users.status` clause — ~3% of members are deactivated with listings in every status, so either rule has data to test it), and pickup ZIP, which I locked equal to the seller's ZIP so a SAME ZIP badge can never appear next to "3.2 mi".

**Claude:**

You're on `main`, up to date at `8f1ca10`. Working tree clean.

## What landed while you were away

Six commits, three PRs, from two teammates:

- **PR #4 — the scaffold.** A whole FastAPI backend (`backend/`) and Next.js frontend (`frontend/`), 53 files. It runs end to end: feed with live facet counts, listing detail with both contact shapes, sign-up, magic-link sign-in, posting, profile.
- **PR #5 — my seed data**, merged into main.
- **PR #6 — the email domain fix.** Billy found that only `@columbia.edu` was admitted, so CBS members couldn't sign up. Four domains are now allowed: `columbia.edu`, `gsb.columbia.edu`, `cumc.columbia.edu`, `tc.columbia.edu`. **This edited `UX_SPEC.md` §1, §4.1, §6.1 and §6.2** — the spec I generated against has changed underneath me.

The README now also assigns scope explicitly: *"Data & analysis | Kobe | The seed generator, the `filter_events` and `enquiries` pipelines, and the five questions in `app/analytics/`."* So the events tables are confirmed mine, and `app/analytics/` is new work that wasn't in my plan.

## Three things this breaks, in order of severity

**1. There are now two seed generators, and they don't share a line of code.** `backend/scripts/seed.py` writes straight to the DB via SQLAlchemy with its own enums (`app/enums.py`), its own ZIP table (`app/services/geo.py`), and its own distributions. Mine writes CSVs from `seed/`. The README's run instructions use theirs. I checked whether they at least agree:

| | backend | `seed/` | |
|---|---|---|---|
| All 8 enums | 8/4/3/14/4/4/3/2 | identical | ✅ agree exactly |
| ZIP table | 18 ZIPs | 47 ZIPs | ⚠️ theirs is a subset of mine |

The enums agreeing is luck — we both transcribed §4.5 faithfully. The ZIP tables differ, which means distance and radius filtering behave differently depending on which seeder ran. That's the kind of divergence that produces a bug nobody can reproduce.

**2. My email generation is now stale.** `seed/vocabularies.py` still has `EMAIL_DOMAIN = "columbia.edu"` and the single-domain regex from the old §4.1. Every one of my 1,000 users has an `@columbia.edu` address, so my corpus never exercises the bug Billy just fixed — and `docs/mock_data_spec.md` quotes the superseded regex in two places.

**3. `docs/mock_data_spec.md` §7 constraint 1 is now wrong** for the same reason.

## What I'd suggest

The duplication is the real issue and it's a team decision, not mine to make unilaterally. Three options, roughly:

- **Mine becomes the source, theirs becomes a loader** — `backend/scripts/seed.py` reads `data/*.csv` instead of generating. Keeps one set of distributions, one ZIP table, and the analysis and the API see the same rows.
- **Theirs stays, mine is retired** — simpler, but loses the validator, the §7 state fixtures, the reference member, and the CSVs the notebook reads.
- **Both stay, explicitly scoped** — theirs for `--reset` dev convenience, mine as the canonical corpus. Needs the ZIP tables reconciled at minimum.

I'd argue for the first, but Jae and Vinayak own the backend so it's their call as much as mine.

Want me to fix the domain staleness in my generator now (it's small — school-issued domains, matching what Billy's seeder already does), and open the duplication question with the team? I haven't touched anything yet.

```
schema is identical on SQLite and Postgres.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import uuid

    DateTime,

    Text,
    UniqueConstraint,
)

    Condition,
    EnquiryChannel,
    Grade,
    ListingStatus,
    School,
```

```
"""Overlap-only disclosure — UX_SPEC.md §5.3.

The single most important rule in the product, and the easiest one to break by
accident. A viewer is shown one of a seller's attributes *only where they
already share it*.

An attribute that does not match is not returned as `false` and not returned as
`null` — it is absent from the payload entirely. If the client ever receives the
seller's raw nationality or school, the rule is broken no matter what the UI
chooses to render.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from ..models import User

SAME_ZIP = "SAME ZIP"
SAME_COUNTRY = "SAME COUNTRY"
SAME_SCHOOL = "SAME SCHOOL"


def badges_for(viewer: User | None, seller: User | None) -> list[str]:
    """Badges to show `viewer` on a listing sold by `seller`.

    Signed-out viewers and external listings both get an empty list: there is no
    overlap to speak of, so nothing is disclosed.
    """
    if viewer is None or seller is None:
        return []
    if viewer.id == seller.id:
        return []  # your own listing needs no badges

    out: list[str] = []
    if viewer.zip_code == seller.zip_code:
        out.append(SAME_ZIP)
    if viewer.nationality == seller.nationality:
        out.append(SAME_COUNTRY)
    if viewer.school == seller.school:
        out.append(SAME_SCHOOL)
    return out


def public_seller(viewer: User | None, seller: User | None) -> dict | None:
    """The seller block for a listing response.

    Everything here is safe for any viewer. Note what is *not* in it: email,
    phone, nationality, school, grade, and the raw ZIP. The contact address and
    number are released only by POST /listings/{id}/enquiry, at the moment the
    buyer taps the button.
    """
    if seller is None:
        return None
    return {
        "username": seller.username,
        "display_name": seller.display_name,
        "is_verified": seller.is_verified,
        "member_since": seller.created_at.isoformat(),
        "badges": badges_for(viewer, seller),
        # Drives the two contact shapes in UX_SPEC.md §5.1. It is a boolean, not
        # the number itself, precisely so the number never reaches the page.
        "can_receive_sms": seller.can_receive_sms,
    }
```

```
def _filtered(
    db: DbSession,
    viewer: User | None,
    *,
    q: str | None,
    category: list[Category],
    subcategory: list[str],
    condition: list[Condition],
    price_min_cents: int | None,
    price_max_cents: int | None,
    radius_mi: float | None,
    same_zip: bool,
    same_nationality: bool,
    same_school: bool,
    source: list[Source],
):
    """One place where every filter is expressed, so the feed and the facet
    counts can never disagree about what a filter means."""
    query = (
        db.query(Listing, Seller)
        .outerjoin(Seller, Listing.seller_id == Seller.id)
        .filter(Listing.status.in_([ListingStatus.ACTIVE, ListingStatus.RESERVED]))
    )

    if q:
        like = f"%{q.strip()}%"
        query = query.filter(or_(Listing.title.ilike(like), Listing.description.ilike(like)))
    if category:
        query = query.filter(Listing.category.in_(category))
    if subcategory:
        query = query.filter(Listing.subcategory.in_(subcategory))
    if condition:
        query = query.filter(Listing.condition.in_(condition))
    if price_min_cents is not None:
        query = query.filter(Listing.price_cents >= price_min_cents)
    if price_max_cents is not None:
        query = query.filter(Listing.price_cents <= price_max_cents)
    if source:
        query = query.filter(Listing.source.in_(source))

    # Radius. Resolved to a ZIP list rather than a per-row distance calculation,
    # so the database can still use its index on listings.zip_code.
    if radius_mi is not None and viewer is not None:
        query = query.filter(Listing.zip_code.in_(geo.zips_within(viewer.zip_code, radius_mi)))

    # Trust filters. Each one implicitly excludes external listings, because an
    # aggregated eBay item has no seller to share anything with. That is the
    # intended behaviour, not a bug: "same country" means a person.
    if viewer is not None:
        if same_zip:
            query = query.filter(Listing.zip_code == viewer.zip_code)
        if same_nationality:
            query = query.filter(Seller.nationality == viewer.nationality)
        if same_school:
            query = query.filter(Seller.school == viewer.school)

    return query
```

```
=== analytics/frames.py ===
"""Load the database into pandas — the entry point for every analysis.

This is a Python course, so the research questions in PROPOSAL.md are answered
here, in pandas, rather than in SQL scattered across the API or in the frontend.
Read the tables once, join in memory, and keep the questions readable.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import pandas as pd

from ..db import engine


def _read(table: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    return pd.read_sql_table(table, engine)


def load() -> dict[str, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Every table, as DataFrames, with the joins the questions need.

    Returns a dict rather than a bag of globals so a notebook can do:

        frames = load()
        listings = frames["listings"]
    """
    users = _read("users")
    listings = _read("listings")
    views = _read("listing_views")
    saves = _read("saves")
    enquiries = _read("enquiries")
    filter_events = _read("filter_events")

    # Everything downstream wants the seller's attributes on the listing row.
    seller_cols = users[["id", "nationality", "school", "grade", "zip_code"]].rename(
        columns={
            "id": "seller_id",
            "nationality": "seller_nationality",
            "school": "seller_school",
            "grade": "seller_grade",
            "zip_code": "seller_zip",
        }
    )
    listings = listings.merge(seller_cols, on="seller_id", how="left")

    listings["is_internal"] = listings["source"].eq("internal")
    listings["price_usd"] = listings["price_cents"] / 100
    listings["posted_at"] = pd.to_datetime(listings["posted_at"], utc=True, errors="coerce")
    listings["sold_at"] = pd.to_datetime(listings["sold_at"], utc=True, errors="coerce")
    listings["days_to_sell"] = (listings["sold_at"] - listings["posted_at"]).dt.total_seconds() / 86400

    for frame, col in ((views, "viewed_at"), (enquiries, "created_at"), (saves, "created_at"), (filter_events, "created_at")):
        if not frame.empty:
            frame[col] = pd.to_datetime(frame[col], utc=True, errors="coerce")

    return {
        "users": users,
        "listings": listings,
        "views": views,
        "saves": saves,
        "enquiries": enquiries,
        "filter_events": filter_events,
```

```
def _price_cents(category: Category) -> tuple[int, bool]:
    if category is Category.FREE_STUFF:
        return 0, True
    if rng.random() < 0.06:  # ~8% of everything ends up free
        return 0, True
    mu, sigma, lo, hi = PRICE_MODEL[category]
    usd = min(max(rng.lognormvariate(mu, sigma), lo), hi)
    return int(round(usd / 5) * 5 * 100), False


def _title(category: Category) -> str:

def _posted_at(now: datetime) -> datetime:
    """Weighted by month so May and August spike."""
    for _ in range(50):
        days_back = rng.randint(0, 420)
        candidate = now - timedelta(days=days_back)
        if rng.random() < MONTH_WEIGHT[candidate.month] / 3.0:
            return candidate
    return now - timedelta(days=rng.randint(0, 420))
```

**Claude:**

Inspection done — no code changed. Here's what I found.

## The shape of the problem

There are now **two independent seed generators**, both claiming UX_SPEC §9, sharing zero code:

| | mine (`seed/` → `data/*.csv`) | theirs (`backend/scripts/seed.py`) |
|---|---|---|
| Writes | CSV + `seed.sql` | straight to the DB via SQLAlchemy |
| ZIP source | `seed/zips.py` — 47 ZIPs | `app/services/geo.py` — 18 ZIPs |
| Enums | `seed/vocabularies.py` | `app/enums.py` |
| Photos | 5,849 rows | none, deliberately |
| Validator | 16 constraint groups | none |

The README's run instructions use theirs. Mine is what `docs/mock_data_spec.md` documents.

**Good news first:** all eight enums match *exactly* — same values, same order, in both files. And their `models.py` column names match my CSV headers on all seven tables. So this is reconcilable, not a rewrite.

## Conflicts, ranked

**1. The ZIP tables — this is the blocker.** Their 18 ZIPs are a strict subset of my 47. Loading my CSVs into their schema means:

- **215 of my 1,000 users (21.5%)** and **390 of my 1,500 listings (26%)** sit in ZIPs `geo.is_supported()` rejects.
- Worse than a validation error: the radius filter resolves through `geo.zips_within()`, so those listings are simply **invisible in every distance-filtered query** — silently, not with an error.
- Where we do overlap, centroids differ slightly: 4 of 17 shared ZIPs disagree by ≥0.1 mi (worst is Williamsburg, 7.1 vs 6.7).

**2. Their `same_zip` filter is a genuine bug.** In `routers/listings.py:96`:

```python
if same_zip:
    query = query.filter(Listing.zip_code == viewer.zip_code)
```

No seller join. The docstring three lines above says *"Each one implicitly excludes external listings"* — true for `same_nationality` and `same_school`, which filter `Seller` columns, but **not** for this one. On my data, an eBay/Facebook listing in 10027 passes the trust filter: `same_zip` returns **379** their way vs **369** mine, and those 10 extra are external listings with no seller to share anything with.

**3. Their grade and school are drawn independently.** `school=rng.choice(SCHOOLS)` and `grade=rng.choice(GRADES)` — so their corpus contains undergraduates at CBS and graduates at Columbia College. 14 of the 42 combinations are ones my generator forbids. Nothing in `models.py` constrains it either.

**4. My email domains are stale.** They now derive the domain from the school — CBS→`gsb`, TC→`tc`, Mailman/VP&S→`cumc` — which is a good idea I should adopt. All 1,000 of my users are `@columbia.edu`, so my corpus never exercises the multi-domain path Billy just fixed.

**5. Their event tables don't hold together.** `savers = rng.sample(users, n_saves)` picks savers unrelated to anyone who viewed, and `Save` has no `created_at` so every save is stamped at seed time. Any time-series or funnel analysis over saves is meaningless on their data. Mine derives each save from an actual view.

**6. Column order.** My `listing_views.csv` is `(id, listing_id, viewer_id, viewed_at, surface)`; the model declares `surface` before `viewed_at`. `\copy` maps by **position**, not header — so the load instructions in my doc need explicit column lists. My bug.

Smaller: their prices have no condition multiplier (a "new" item costs the same as "used — fair"); their `posted_at` can precede the seller's `created_at`; their phone numbers use `555-1xxx`, outside the reserved fictional block; every username is `cu_0000`…`cu_0999` with `display_name` always null.

**And one of mine to correct:** `mock_data_spec.md` claims a username sits at exactly 20 chars. The longest actually generated is 19. The edge case I wrote about doesn't exist.

## What I'd suggest

**Make the backend the single source for shared facts, and my generator the single source for rows.** Concretely:

1. **One ZIP table.** Extend `app/services/geo.py` to my 47 — theirs is a subset, so nothing breaks, and §4.6 asks for ~42. Then delete `seed/zips.py`'s table and have my generator import from the backend, so there is one list and one set of centroids.
2. **`backend/scripts/seed.py` becomes a loader**, not a generator — read `data/*.csv` and insert. Keeps the CLI the README documents (`--reset` still works), and deletes ~360 lines of duplicated distributions along with problems 3 and 5.
3. **Fix the `same_zip` filter** to join the seller, matching its own docstring and my reference implementation.
4. **I adopt their school→domain mapping** and fix the column order and the two doc errors.

That leaves one deliberate difference worth keeping: my pickup ZIP is locked equal to the seller's ZIP. Their code needs that — the badge reads `seller.zip_code` while the filter reads `Listing.zip_code`, so if those ever diverge, a listing shows SAME ZIP next to a three-mile distance. Locking them makes it unrepresentable.

Items 1 and 3 are Jae/Vinayak's call since it's their code. Items 2 and 4 I can do now. Want me to start, or take this to the team first?

```bash
# list, those listings were invisible to every distance query rather than failing
# loudly. One table, one place.
#
# Loaded by path rather than imported as a package: `backend/` is a separate
# deployable with its own dependencies, and this keeps the generator from
# depending on anything installed over there. geo.py imports only `dataclasses`
# and `math`, so this stays cheap.

_GEO_PATH = os.path.normpath(
    os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), os.pardir,
                 "backend", "app", "services", "geo.py")
)


def _load_backend_geo():
    if not os.path.exists(_GEO_PATH):
        raise RuntimeError(
            "Cannot find the ZIP table at %s. It is the single source of truth "
            "for ZIP codes and centroids; if the backend moved, update _GEO_PATH "
            "rather than pasting the table back into this file." % _GEO_PATH
        )
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("_backend_geo", _GEO_PATH)
    module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(module)
    return module

)
```

**Claude:**

The dataclass needs the module registered in `sys.modules` before exec — classic pitfall with path-loading.


> **`Edit`**

> `/Users/kobeko/Desktop/MBA:MS/Python_bootcamp/secondhand_marketplace/seed/zips.py`

> _old_string_

```
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("_backend_geo", _GEO_PATH)
    module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(module)
    return module
```

> _new_string_

```
    name = "_backend_geo"
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name, _GEO_PATH)
    module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    # Register before executing: geo.py declares a @dataclass, and dataclasses
    # resolves field types through sys.modules[cls.__module__]. Without this the
    # import dies with "NoneType has no attribute __dict__".
    sys.modules[name] = module
    spec.loader.exec_module(module)
    return module
```

> _new_string_

```
# §4.1, as amended by the multi-domain fix. Four whole domains, never a suffix
# test: endswith("@columbia.edu") rejects @gsb.columbia.edu, and a looser suffix
# match against a bare columbia.edu would admit @evil-columbia.edu.
# backend/app/config.py is authoritative and publishes the list at
# /reference/enums; this copy exists so the generator has no backend dependency.
EMAIL_DOMAINS: tuple[str, ...] = (
    "columbia.edu",
    "gsb.columbia.edu",
    "cumc.columbia.edu",
    "tc.columbia.edu",
)
EMAIL_PATTERN = r"^[a-z0-9._%+-]+@(?:%s)$" % "|".join(
    d.replace(".", r"\.") for d in EMAIL_DOMAINS
)

# Schools that issue their own address; everyone else is on plain columbia.edu.
# Seeding all four means the multi-domain sign-in path is exercised by the data
# rather than only by a hand-typed test -- the same argument §9 makes for the
# ~30% NULL phone numbers.
SCHOOL_EMAIL_DOMAIN: dict[str, str] = {
    "cbs": "gsb.columbia.edu",
    "teachers_college": "tc.columbia.edu",
    "public_health": "cumc.columbia.edu",
    "vps": "cumc.columbia.edu",
}


def email_domain_for(school: str) -> str:
    """The address a school issues. Mirrors backend/scripts/seed.py."""
    return SCHOOL_EMAIL_DOMAIN.get(school, "columbia.edu")
```

```
"""Load the generated corpus into the database — UX_SPEC.md §9.

    python -m scripts.seed --reset                    # load data/*.csv
    python -m scripts.seed --reset --regenerate       # rebuild the CSVs first
    python -m scripts.seed --reset --users 2000 --listings 3000   # implies --regenerate

This used to generate its own rows. It no longer does, and that is deliberate:
there were two generators claiming the same §9, and they had already drifted.
The ZIP tables disagreed (18 codes here, 47 in the generator), grade and school
were drawn independently here so undergraduates appeared at CBS, and saves were
sampled from users who had never viewed the listing, which made every time-based
analysis over `saves` meaningless.

The corpus now comes from `seed/`, at the repository root, which owns the
distributions, a 16-group validator and the §7 state fixtures. This file is the
loader. See docs/mock_data_spec.md.

Everything about *how* the data looks belongs in `seed/`. Everything about how it
reaches Postgres or SQLite belongs here.
"""

    return value.strip().lower() in ("true", "t", "1", "yes")


def _int(value: str) -> int:
    return int(value) if value != "" else 0


def _float(value: str) -> float:
    return float(value) if value != "" else 0.0


def _dt(value: str):
    """ISO-8601 with an offset, as written by seed/export.py."""
    if not value:
        return None
    return datetime.fromisoformat(value)


def _text(value: str):
    """Empty field means NULL — the convention seed/export.py writes."""
    return value if value != "" else None


def _read(name: str) -> list[dict]:
    path = os.path.join(DATA_DIR, name)
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        raise SystemExit(
            "%s not found.\n"
            "Generate the corpus first:  python3 -m seed.generate\n"
            "or re-run this with --regenerate." % path
```

## How to run it

**1. See the corpus without writing anything** — this is the one I'd start with:


**2. Inspect individual pieces:**


**4. Then load into the app:**

```bash

```

`--reset --regenerate` does steps 3 and 4 in one go, and `--users N --listings N` implies `--regenerate`.

## Two things to know before you run step 3

**`data/` is currently stale.** The CSVs on disk still have the old single-domain emails and the old `listing_views` column order. They'll load, but they won't exercise the multi-domain path. Step 3 fixes that.

**The reference member keeps `dl3729@columbia.edu`** even though they're CBS and the rule would issue `@gsb`. That's deliberate — it's the address the account-settings mockup shows, it's true to life (a CBS student holds a general UNI address too), and it means the fixture covers the case where school and email domain don't imply each other. I left a comment saying so in `seed/edge_cases.py` so nobody "fixes" it later.

One thing I did **not** touch: their `_price_cents` has no condition multiplier, so on their old generator a "new" item cost the same as "used — fair". That's now moot since the generator is gone, but if anyone revives it, it's worth knowing.

**Claude:**

Two separate problems, and the first one is a genuine gotcha.

**1. Your project folder is named `MBA:MS` — the colon breaks venv activation.**

`PATH` entries are separated by colons. When `source .venv/bin/activate` prepends the venv's `bin` directory, the shell splits it in half:

```
/Users/kobeko/Desktop/MBA          ← nonsense
MS/Python_bootcamp/.../.venv/bin   ← nonsense
```

So the venv's `pip` and `python` are never on `PATH`, and you get `command not found: pip`. Nothing was wrong with what you typed.

**2. You only have Python 3.9.6**, and `requirements.txt` pins `numpy==2.2.1`, which needs Python ≥ 3.10. The backend README asks for 3.12 or 3.13. (No venv was created either — `backend/.venv` doesn't exist.)

## The fix

Install a newer Python and put the venv *outside* the colon path:


> **`Bash`**

> Check for brew-installed Python versions

```bash
brew list --formula 2>/dev/null | grep -i "^python" || echo "no brew python formulae installed"; echo "---"; ls /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.* 2>/dev/null || echo "no brew pythons in /opt/homebrew/bin"
```

<details><summary>result</summary>


```
no brew python formulae installed
---
(eval):1: no matches found: /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.*
no brew pythons in /opt/homebrew/bin
```


</details>


**Claude:**

No Homebrew Python installed — only Apple's 3.9. Here's the corrected sequence.

**Install a supported Python** (run this yourself so you see the progress — it takes a few minutes):

```
! brew install python@3.12
```

**Then create the venv outside the colon path.** This is the key change from the README's instructions:

```bash
/opt/homebrew/bin/python3.12 -m venv ~/.venvs/columbia-market
source ~/.venvs/columbia-market/bin/activate
cd "/Users/kobeko/Desktop/MBA:MS/Python_bootcamp/secondhand_marketplace/backend"
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env
python -m scripts.seed --reset
uvicorn app.main:app --reload
```

The venv lives at `~/.venvs/columbia-market`, which has no colon in it, so activation works normally and `pip` resolves. Your project stays exactly where it is.

**Alternative if you'd rather fix it permanently:** rename the folder from `MBA:MS` to `MBA-MS`. A colon in a directory name will keep biting you — it breaks `PATH`, and it also breaks some Makefiles, `PYTHONPATH`, and a few CLI tools. Then the README's instructions work verbatim. Downside is you'd re-clone or re-point anything referencing the old path.

Two smaller notes:

- Don't use `python3 -m venv backend/.venv` — even created successfully, activating it hits the same colon problem. If you want it inside the project anyway, skip activation and call the binaries directly: `backend/.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt`, then `backend/.venv/bin/uvicorn app.main:app --reload`.
- Once you're running, sign in as `dl3729@columbia.edu`. In dev the magic link comes back in the API response and the console rather than by email. That user should see 789 listings within 2.5 miles.

## It's live

- **App:** http://localhost:3000 — you're already signed in as `@brian_dw` in the Chrome tab
- **API:** http://localhost:8001 — docs at http://localhost:8001/docs

**Port 8000 was already taken by your Wordcraft project** (running since Sep 1), so I put Columbia Market on 8001 and wrote `frontend/.env.local` pointing at it. I left Wordcraft alone.

## What I installed

- Homebrew **Python 3.12.14** (you only had Apple's 3.9, too old for `numpy==2.2.1`)
- Homebrew **Node 26.8.1** + npm — neither was installed
- A venv at **`~/.venvs/columbia-market`**, deliberately *outside* the project

## The colon problem is real and it bit twice

Your folder is `MBA:MS`, and `PATH` is colon-separated. It broke `source .venv/bin/activate` (your original `pip: command not found`) and then broke `npm run dev` the same way — npm puts `node_modules/.bin` on `PATH`, which split at the colon and gave `sh: next: command not found`.

Both are worked around: the venv lives outside the project, and I start Next.js via `./node_modules/.bin/next dev` rather than the npm script. **Renaming `MBA:MS` to `MBA-MS` would remove the whole class of problem** — it'll keep surfacing in new tools.

## Verified end to end

Every facet count from the live API matched my generator's prediction exactly — all 13 of them: 789 within 2.5 mi, 369 same-ZIP, 91 same-nationality, 154 same-school, and all eight category counts. My `seed/feed.py` and their `routers/listings.py` are independent implementations of §5.4 and they agree perfectly. That's the cross-check worth having.

Also confirmed in the browser: match badges render, the funnel counters show, descriptions match their conditions, Korean sellers have Korean names, gmail is rejected at sign-in while `gsb.columbia.edu` is accepted, the 60-second resend lock works, and the `D12` email-only contact shape renders correctly.

**One fix along the way:** the reference member's trust-filter defaults came out of a random draw as same-ZIP *on*, which contradicted the account-settings mockup and opened the demo feed pre-narrowed to one ZIP. I pinned them to what the design shows — same-ZIP off, same-nationality on — regenerated and reloaded.

## Two things to know

**Nothing is committed.** 16 modified files sit on `main`, including the backend changes to `geo.py`, `listings.py` and `scripts/seed.py` that Jae and Vinayak own. You'll want a branch before committing, and the `same_zip` fix in particular deserves a heads-up to them.

**Next.js auto-generated `frontend/AGENTS.md` and `frontend/CLAUDE.md`** on first run — untracked, not mine. Delete them or commit them, but decide deliberately; they weren't there before.

To stop the servers: `kill 70988 72483`.

```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Render the placeholder photos referenced by ``listing_photos.url``.

The images are *not* committed — there are ~5,800 of them and they carry no
information. This script rebuilds them from the CSV, deterministically, so two
people running it get the same pictures.

    python3 scripts/make_photos.py --out frontend/public/photos

Each photo is a 135° gradient in one of the ``01 · Foundations`` tints — the same
angle and palette as the ``.photo-placeholder`` rule in ``frontend/app/globals.css``,
so a missing file degrades to something that looks deliberate rather than broken.
The colour comes from a hash of the listing id, so a listing's gallery is a
coherent set and the same listing always gets the same colour; later positions
step through the palette so a five-photo gallery reads as five shots rather than
five copies.

The category is drawn as an overline in the corner, matching the feed card, and
the item title sits under it. That is as far as this goes: these are honest
placeholders, not fake photographs of things that do not exist.

Pillow is required for the WebP files the URLs name. Without it the script writes
SVGs beside them and says so.
"""

    ((0xEE, 0xDF, 0xC4), (0xD8, 0xBE, 0x92)),   # sand
    ((0xDD, 0xE0, 0xEC), (0xB9, 0xBF, 0xD4)),   # slate
    ((0xD6, 0xE8, 0xDA), (0xA6, 0xC9, 0xB0)),   # sage
    ((0xF4, 0xDD, 0xDD), (0xDE, 0xB0, 0xB0)),   # blush
    ((0xE4, 0xDC, 0xEF), (0xC0, 0xB0, 0xDC)),   # lilac
    ((0xE6, 0xE6, 0xE6), (0xBB, 0xBB, 0xBB)),   # neutral
)

WIDTH, HEIGHT = 800, 600
QUALITY = 78

# Ink for the overline and title, from color/text/* in UX_SPEC §3.1.
INK = (0x2A, 0x3A, 0x52)
INK_SOFT = (0x4A, 0x5B, 0x74)

_FONT_CANDIDATES = (

)


def _palette_for(listing_id: str, position: int):
    digest = hashlib.sha256(listing_id.encode()).digest()
    return GRADIENTS[(digest[0] + position) % len(GRADIENTS)]
```

```
export default function ListingPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = use(params);
  const [me, setMe] = useState<Me | null>(null);
  const [listing, setListing] = useState<ListingDetail | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {

    api.listing(id).then(setListing).catch(() => setListing(null));

      </>
    );
  }
```

The images load — but now there's a collision: my baked-in category/title text is colliding with the card's own overline, so it reads doubled. The text shouldn't be in the image at all — the frontend already draws it. Replacing it with category line-art instead:

```bash
cd "/Users/kobeko/Desktop/MBA:MS/Python_bootcamp/secondhand_marketplace" && python3 - <<'PY'
p = "scripts/make_photos.py"
s = open(p, encoding="utf-8").read()

# --- docstring: describe glyphs, not text ---
s = s.replace(
"""The category is drawn as an overline in the corner, matching the feed card, and
the item title sits under it. That is as far as this goes: these are honest
placeholders, not fake photographs of things that do not exist.""",
"""A simple line drawing of the category sits in the middle — a book, a desk, a
bicycle. Deliberately *not* text: the feed card already draws the category as an
overline and the title underneath it, so baking either into the image renders it
twice, overlapping. These are honest placeholders, not fake photographs of things
that do not exist.""")

# --- replace the font machinery with glyph geometry ---
old_fonts = '''# Ink for the overline and title, from color/text/* in UX_SPEC §3.1.
INK = (0x2A, 0x3A, 0x52)
INK_SOFT = (0x4A, 0x5B, 0x74)

_FONT_CANDIDATES = (
    "/System/Library/Fonts/Supplemental/Helvetica.ttc",
    "/System/Library/Fonts/Helvetica.ttc",
    "/System/Library/Fonts/HelveticaNeue.ttc",
    "/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans.ttf",
)
'''
new_fonts = '''# Glyph ink: color/text/primary at low alpha, so the drawing reads as a watermark
# on every one of the seven tints rather than fighting the lighter ones.
GLYPH_INK = (0x11, 0x19, 0x27, 64)
STROKE = 7
GLYPH_BOX = 300  # the square the drawing is fitted into, centred on the canvas
'''
assert old_fonts in s
s = s.replace(old_fonts, new_fonts)

open(p, "w", encoding="utf-8").write(s)
print("header rewritten")
PY
```

```
# Each takes a drawing context and a square (x, y, size) and draws inside it.
# Primitives on purpose: no font dependency, no asset files, and it renders
# identically on every machine.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def _book(d, x, y, s):
    d.line([(x + s * 0.5, y + s * 0.18), (x + s * 0.5, y + s * 0.86)], GLYPH_INK, STROKE)
    for side in (-1, 1):
        cx = x + s * 0.5
        outer = cx + side * s * 0.42
        d.line([(cx, y + s * 0.18), (outer, y + s * 0.28)], GLYPH_INK, STROKE)
        d.line([(outer, y + s * 0.28), (outer, y + s * 0.80)], GLYPH_INK, STROKE)
        d.line([(cx, y + s * 0.86), (outer, y + s * 0.80)], GLYPH_INK, STROKE)


def _desk(d, x, y, s):
    d.line([(x + s * 0.06, y + s * 0.36), (x + s * 0.94, y + s * 0.36)], GLYPH_INK, STROKE)
    d.line([(x + s * 0.16, y + s * 0.36), (x + s * 0.16, y + s * 0.84)], GLYPH_INK, STROKE)
    d.line([(x + s * 0.84, y + s * 0.36), (x + s * 0.84, y + s * 0.84)], GLYPH_INK, STROKE)
    d.rectangle([x + s * 0.28, y + s * 0.44, x + s * 0.62, y + s * 0.60],
                outline=GLYPH_INK, width=STROKE - 2)


def _laptop(d, x, y, s):
    d.rectangle([x + s * 0.16, y + s * 0.22, x + s * 0.84, y + s * 0.64],
                outline=GLYPH_INK, width=STROKE)
    d.line([(x + s * 0.04, y + s * 0.78), (x + s * 0.96, y + s * 0.78)], GLYPH_INK, STROKE)
    d.line([(x + s * 0.16, y + s * 0.64), (x + s * 0.04, y + s * 0.78)], GLYPH_INK, STROKE)
    d.line([(x + s * 0.84, y + s * 0.64), (x + s * 0.96, y + s * 0.78)], GLYPH_INK, STROKE)


def _mug(d, x, y, s):
    d.rectangle([x + s * 0.20, y + s * 0.34, x + s * 0.64, y + s * 0.82],
                outline=GLYPH_INK, width=STROKE)
    d.arc([x + s * 0.58, y + s * 0.44, x + s * 0.88, y + s * 0.68], -90, 90,

    for i in range(2):
        sx = x + s * (0.32 + i * 0.18)
        d.line([(sx, y + s * 0.24), (sx, y + s * 0.10)], GLYPH_INK, STROKE - 2)


def _shirt(d, x, y, s):
```

```
            "url": "/photos/%s/%d.webp" % (listing_id, position),
```

**Claude:**

Images are filled and the gallery works — clicking a thumbnail swaps the main photo, and the selected one takes the Columbia-blue border.

## What was actually wrong

Three separate causes, not one:

1. **`frontend/public/` didn't exist**, so every `photos/…` request 404'd. The gradient you saw was the CSS fallback, not an image.
2. **The detail page rendered no `<img>` at all** — just the placeholder div. Even with files present it would have shown nothing.
3. **The photo URLs were relative** (`photos/…`), so they resolved to `/listings/photos/…` on a detail page. This one only became visible *after* I fixed the first two — the feed worked, the detail page showed broken-image icons.

## What I did

- **Rewrote `scripts/make_photos.py`** to draw a category glyph — desk, book, laptop, mug, shirt, bicycle, dumbbell, gift — over the 135° gradient, on the same palette as `.photo-placeholder` in `globals.css`. Generated all **5,849 images (23 MB) in 66 seconds**.
- **Added the gallery to the detail page**, with a thumbnail strip that only appears when there's more than one photo (state `D1`), keyboard-focusable buttons, and the gradient kept underneath as a fallback.
- **Made the URLs root-relative** in `seed/listings.py`, regenerated the CSVs and reloaded the database.
- **Restored the `photos/` ignore rule** — it was silently lost when the branches merged, so those 5,849 files would otherwise have been committed.

My first attempt baked the category and title *into* the image, which collided with the card's own overline and read as doubled text. That's why it's line-art now: the frontend already draws the words, so the image shouldn't.

One judgement call worth flagging: I edited `frontend/app/listings/[id]/page.tsx`, which is Brian's file per the README's ownership table. The change is small and additive — one `useState` and a gallery block — but it's his to review.

To regenerate after any data change:

```bash
python3 -m seed.generate
~/.venvs/columbia-market/bin/python scripts/make_photos.py --out frontend/public/photos
cd backend && ~/.venvs/columbia-market/bin/python -m scripts.seed --reset
```

Still uncommitted — 18 modified files across `seed/`, `backend/`, `frontend/`, `data/` and the docs.

## 20. Kobe — 2026-09-02 20:29

I checked it but its not a real image. Would changing this to "real image" cost a lot?


**Claude:**

Short answer: **no, it's cheap** — maybe half an hour of work and no new infrastructure. The generator already separates *which* photo a listing points at from *what that file contains*, so swapping the renderer for a downloader touches one script.

The real costs aren't effort, they're these three:

- **Repetition.** 1,500 listings need 1,500 cover photos. Nobody hands you 1,500 distinct free photos of student furniture, so you reuse — with ~400 photos each cover repeats ~4 times in the grid, which is noticeable if you scroll.
- **Licensing.** Real photos need a source whose licence permits this, plus an attribution file. That rules out scraping image search.
- **Network + weight.** Downloading is a one-off script, but the repo either grows or the photos stay gitignored and each teammate downloads them once (~50–150 MB).

One thing I want to flag before you choose: I need your go-ahead to download files from an external service either way.

What would you like to clarify?

Happy to answer anything before you pick — but a few things I can guess at, in case one of these is the sticking point:

- **What "real image" means to you.** Actual photographs of desks and textbooks? Or would category-correct illustrations be enough, just more finished-looking than the thin line-art I made?
- **What the images are for.** A demo you'll click through, screenshots in a report, or just so the page doesn't look broken? That changes the answer a lot — random-subject photos are fine for the third and bad for the second.
- **Whether the repetition matters.** Four listings showing the same stock desk photo is the unavoidable part of any free-photo approach at 1,500 listings. If that's a dealbreaker, it's worth knowing now.
- **Whether the download itself is the concern** — network dependency, licensing, repo size, or teammates needing to run an extra command.

Or if it's something else entirely, just say.

**Claude:**

**Yes, and here's why it's cheap:** the corpus isn't 1,500 unique things. It's generated from **50 templates** covering **105 distinct nouns**, producing 424 distinct titles. So I attach a search query to each *template*, not each listing — about 90 queries total.

That means the query can carry the title's own attributes, because they come from the same slots:

| Title | Query it would fetch |
|---|---|
| `IKEA MALM desk 140×65, white` | white wooden desk |
| `Cuckoo 6-cup rice cooker, barely used` | rice cooker |
| `Canada Goose parka, size M` | winter parka coat |
| `Trek FX 2, M frame` | hybrid bicycle |
| `Corporate Finance (Berk) 5th ed.` | stack of textbooks |

**The honest limitation:** free photo libraries won't have brand-exact shots. A "Herman Miller Aeron, size B" listing gets a real photo of a black mesh office chair, not an actual Aeron. The *kind of thing and its main attribute* will match; the brand won't. If that gap bothers you, the alternative is loosening the titles — but I'd keep the good titles and accept a generic chair.

```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fetch real photos from Pexels that match what each listing actually is.

    python3 scripts/fetch_photos.py --fraction 0.1     # a sample, to judge quality
    python3 scripts/fetch_photos.py                    # everything

Why this works without 1,500 searches: the corpus is generated from ~75 item
templates, and each template carries its own search query (see
``seed/catalog.py``). ``seed.generate`` writes the per-listing query to
``data/photo_queries.csv``, so a listing titled "IKEA MALM desk 140x65, white"
asks for "white wooden desk" and one titled "Cuckoo 6-cup rice cooker" asks for
"rice cooker". Roughly 75 searches cover the whole catalogue.

Two pools, kept apart on purpose:

``data/photo_pool/<query>/<n>.jpg``
    Downloaded originals, one directory per query. Cached, so re-running does not
    re-download, and so switching which listing gets which photo costs nothing.

``frontend/public/photos/<listing_id>/<position>.webp``
    What the app serves, resized and re-encoded. Assignment is by a hash of the
    listing id, so it is deterministic and a listing keeps the same photo across
    runs.

Anything a search cannot fill falls back to ``scripts/make_photos.py``'s glyph,
so the app never shows a broken image. Credits are written to
``data/PHOTO_CREDITS.csv``: the Pexels licence does not require attribution, but
recording where a file came from is cheap and makes the licence auditable.

The API key is read from ``backend/.env`` (``PEXELS_API_KEY=...``) or the
environment. It is never printed and never written anywhere else.
"""

OUT_W, OUT_H = 800, 600

                    return line.split("=",
```
