**Claude:**

Everything's built and waiting on one thing: **your Pexels API key.**

## What I need from you

Get a free key at https://www.pexels.com/api/ (sign in, click "Get Started" — takes about two minutes), then add one line to `backend/.env`:

```
PEXELS_API_KEY=your_key_here
```

Add it in your editor rather than pasting it here, so it doesn't end up in this transcript. The script reads it from that file, never prints it, and `.env` is already gitignored. I won't create the account or handle the key myself.

Then tell me and I'll run:

```
python3 scripts/fetch_photos.py --fraction 0.1
```

## What that trial will do

- **140 listings** (a deterministic 10% slice — whole galleries, not partial ones)
- **65 distinct searches**, well inside the free tier's 200/hour
- ~8 photos pooled per query, cached in `data/photo_pool/` so the remaining 90% costs no re-downloading

## What changed while building it

The real work was in the catalog. Templates that hid several objects behind one slot had to be split — `{kitchen_small}` covered a rice cooker, a blender and a kettle, and no single search matches all three. That took the catalog from 50 templates to **75**, each with its own query:

| Title | Searches for |
|---|---|
| `IKEA MALM desk 140×65, white` | white wooden desk |
| `Cuckoo 6-cup rice cooker, barely used` | rice cooker |
| `Canada Goose parka, size M` | winter parka coat |
| `HON Ignition, size C` | black mesh office chair |

Title and query are filled from **one** slot resolution, so a listing that says "white" can't fetch a photo of an oak one.

`seed.generate` now also writes `data/photo_queries.csv` (1,500 rows) — generator metadata, deliberately kept out of `listings.csv` since UX_SPEC §4.2 has no such column and the database shouldn't grow one. All 16 invariants still pass.

Two things I built in deliberately: anything a search can't fill **falls back to the category glyph**, so the app never shows a broken image; and credits go to `data/PHOTO_CREDITS.csv` — the Pexels licence doesn't require attribution, but recording provenance makes it auditable.

The honest caveat stands: you'll get a real photo of a black mesh office chair, not an actual Herman Miller Aeron. Judge that on the sample.

**Claude:**

Depends which "it" you mean — here's both.

## Right now, with no key: the app is already live

Both servers are still up. Open **http://localhost:3000** and you'll see the current state — 1,500 listings with the line-art glyph images. That's what we're trying to improve on, so it's a useful baseline to compare against.

## To check the real photos: three steps

**1. Get the key** — https://www.pexels.com/api/ → sign in → "Get Started". It gives you a long string on screen.

**2. Put it in `backend/.env`.** Open that file in your editor and add one line at the bottom:

```
PEXELS_API_KEY=paste_the_long_string_here
```

Save. That file is already gitignored, so it won't be committed. I'd rather you paste it there than into this chat.

**3. Say "go"** and I'll run the 10% sample, then refresh the browser and show you screenshots.

If you want to confirm the key works before the full sample, I can run a single search first — one request, one photo, five seconds.

## What to actually look at when judging

Once it's rendered, three things decide whether it's worth doing the other 90%:

- **The feed grid** at http://localhost:3000 — this is where repetition shows. With ~8 photos per query, a category with many listings will repeat. If it reads as obviously duplicated, we bump `--per-query` up.
- **A detail page gallery** — click any card. Its 3–5 photos should look like different shots of the same *kind* of thing, not one photo four times.
- **The weak categories specifically.** Textbooks and kitchen appliances are where free stock libraries are thinnest. Filter to Textbooks in the sidebar and see whether "college textbook" returned something plausible or something odd.

The sample covers 140 listings across 65 queries, so every category will be represented.

One thing worth deciding after you look: whether a wrong-but-real photo is better or worse than a right-but-abstract glyph. A generic office chair on a "Herman Miller Aeron" listing is honest enough; a random armchair on a "Yoga mat + blocks" listing would not be. That's the judgement the sample exists to let you make.

## What was actually broken

Not the photos — **the database was stale**. Adding the photo-query field changed the RNG stream, so regenerating produced new listing UUIDs, but I hadn't reloaded the DB. Only 7 of 24 listings on screen still matched the CSV, so the rest asked for `/photos/<old-id>/…` and got nothing. Reloaded, and it's 24 of 24.

That's my mistake and worth a guard — right now nothing warns you when `data/` is newer than the database.

## No API key needed

I switched the default source to **Openverse**, which aggregates openly-licensed photos from Flickr and Wikimedia with no account at all. 92 searches, 493 originals pooled, **5,786 photos rendered**, every query returned results — zero fell back to glyphs. Licences restricted to `cc0`, `by` and `by-sa`, with provenance in `data/PHOTO_CREDITS.csv`.

Pexels is still supported via `--source pexels` if you ever want the better-looking library.

## Honest assessment of the quality

Scroll and you'll see the trade. It's genuinely mixed:

- **Good:** headphones, monitors, suits, toaster ovens, sneakers — anything with a clear canonical look.
- **Rough:** these are Flickr photos, not product shots. The futon sofa is a mattress propped against a car in someone's yard. Lighting and framing are inconsistent, and it reads more like a real second-hand marketplace than a catalogue — which may actually suit this product.
- **Repetition:** ~6 photos per query, so a category with 30 listings repeats. Raise it with `--per-query 12` if it bothers you.

**212 MB** on disk, gitignored, rebuilt with one command.

Two things worth knowing before you decide to keep this: the pool is another 120 MB in `data/photo_pool/` (also gitignored), and if you'd rather go back, `python3 scripts/make_photos.py --out frontend/public/photos` restores the glyphs in about a minute.

Photos are **100% complete** — 5,786 of 5,786, nothing missing. But the audit found a real defect worth fixing first: five searches returned only one usable photo, so **31 office-chair listings all show the identical image**.

Fixing that by topping thin pools up from Wikimedia rather than only falling back when a search returns nothing:


> **`Bash`**

> Deepen the photo pools

```bash
cd "/Users/kobeko/Desktop/MBA:MS/Python_bootcamp/secondhand_marketplace" && python3 - <<'PY'
p="scripts/fetch_photos.py"; s=open(p, encoding="utf-8").read()
old = '''        photos = search(source, key, query, per_query)
        if not photos and source == "openverse":
            photos = _search_wikimedia(query, per_query)'''
new = '''        photos = search(source, key, query, per_query)
        # Top up rather than only falling back on zero. Under the cc0/by/by-sa
        # licence filter some ordinary objects return one or two results, and a
        # single photo shared by 31 office-chair listings is worse than a mixed
        # pool: the grid reads as one item posted 31 times.
        if source == "openverse" and len(photos) < per_query:
            seen = {p["src"] for p in photos}
            for extra in _search_wikimedia(query, per_query - len(photos)):
                if extra["src"] not in seen:
                    photos.append(extra)'''
assert old in s
open(p,"w", encoding="utf-8").write(s.replace(old,new,1)); print("top-up added")
```

```
/**
 * The one place that talks to the API.
 *
 * `credentials: "include"` on every call, because auth is a session cookie —
 * there is no token to attach and no password to store.
 */

import type {
  FacetCounts,
  FeedFilters,
  ListingDetail,
  ListingPage,
  Me,
  ZipResult,
} from "./types";

const BASE = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE ?? "http://localhost:8000";

export class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(
    public status: number,
    message: string,
  ) {
    super(message);
  }
}

async function request<T>(path: string, init: RequestInit = {}): Promise<T> {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}${path}`, {
    credentials: "include",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", ...(init.headers ?? {}) },
    ...init,
  });

  if (!res.ok) {
    const body = await res.json().catch(() => ({}));
    throw new ApiError(res.status, body.detail ?? res.statusText);
  }
  return res.status === 204 ? (undefined as T) : ((await res.json()) as T);
}

function qs(filters: FeedFilters): string {
  const p = new URLSearchParams();
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(filters)) {
    if (value === undefined || value === null || value === "" || value === false) continue;
    if (Array.isArray(value)) value.forEach((v) => p.append(key, String(v)));
    else p.set(key, String(value));
  }
  const s = p.toString();
  return s ? `?${s}` : "";
}
```

```bash
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The three "my stuff" collections behind the avatar menu (UX_SPEC.md §6.6).
#
# All of them reuse `to_card` from the listings router, so a card looks and
# behaves identically wherever it appears -- same badges, same distance, same
# overlap-only disclosure. Importing it here rather than duplicating the
# serialiser is the whole point.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def _page(rows, viewer, total, limit, offset) -> ListingPage:
    from .listings import to_card

    return ListingPage(
        items=[to_card(listing, seller, viewer) for listing, seller in rows],
        total=total,
        limit=limit,
        offset=offset,
    )


@router.get("/listings", response_model=ListingPage)
def my_listings(
    limit: int = 24,
    offset: int = 0,
    user: User = Depends(current_user),
    db: DbSession = Depends(get_db),
):
    """Everything this member has posted, in every status.

    Deliberately unfiltered by status: drafts and sold items are exactly what the
    owner came here to see, even though the feed hides both.
    """
    query = (
        db.query(Listing, User)
        .join(User, Listing.seller_id == User.id)
        .filter(Listing.seller_id == user.id)
    )
    total = query.count()
    rows = query.order_by(desc(Listing.posted_at)).offset(offset).limit(limit).all()
    return _page(rows, user, total, limit, offset)


@router.get("/saves", response_model=ListingPage)
def my_saves(
    limit: int = 24,
    offset: int = 0,
    user: User = Depends(current_user),
    db: DbSession = Depends(get_db),
):
    """Saved items, newest save first.

    A save outlives the listing's availability, so sold and reserved rows stay
    here -- vanishing silently when a seller marks something sold would read as
    data loss.
    """
    Seller = aliased(User)
    query = (
        db.query(Listing, Seller)
        .join(Save, Save.listing_id == Listing.id)
        .outerjoin(Seller, Listing.seller_id == Seller.id)
        .filter(Save.user_id == user.id)
    )
    total = query.count()
    rows = query.order_by(desc(Save.created_at)).offset(offset).limit(limit).all()
    return _page(rows, user, total, limit, offset)
```

```
"use client";

import Link from "next/link";
import type { ReactNode } from "react";

import { ItemCard, ItemRow } from "@/components/ItemCard";
import { MobileTabBar, TopNav } from "@/components/TopNav";
import type { ListingCard, Me } from "@/lib/types";

/**
 * The shell behind Saved items, My listings and Inbox — UX_SPEC.md §6.6.
 *
 * All three are the same shape: a heading, a count, and a grid of the same cards
 * the feed uses. Sharing the shell is what keeps a card identical wherever it
 * appears — same badges, same distance, same overlap-only disclosure — because
 * every one of them renders `ItemCard` off a `ListingCard` the API serialised.
 *
 * The empty state is a first-class argument, not an afterthought: these three
 * screens are empty for most members most of the time, so "nothing here yet" is
 * the common case and needs to say what to do about it.
 */
export function CollectionPage({
  me,
  title,
  blurb,
  loading,
  total,
  items,
  empty,
  children,
}: {
  me: Me | null;
  title: string;
  blurb: string;
  loading: boolean;
  total: number;
  items?: ListingCard[];
  empty: { headline: string; body: string; cta?: { href: string; label: string } };
  children?: ReactNode;
}) {
  const isEmpty = !loading && total === 0;

  return (
    <>
      <TopNav me={me} />

      <main className="mx-auto max-w-[1360px] px-4 py-7 pb-24 md:px-10 md:pb-7">
        <header className="mb-6 flex flex-col gap-1.5">
          <h1 className="text-[26px] font-bold tracking-[-0.02em] md:text-[32px]">{title}</h1>
          <p className="max-w-[62ch] text-[14.5px] leading-[23px] text-ink2">{blurb}</p>
          {!loading && total > 0 && (
            <p className="pt-1 text-[13px] font-semibold text-ink2">
              {total} {total === 1 ? "item" : "items"}
            </p>
          )}
        </header>

        {loading && <p className="py-16 text-center text-[14.5px] text-ink2">Loading…</p>}

        {isEmpty && (
          <div className="flex flex-col items-center gap-3 rounded-[16px] border border-line bg-surface px-6 py-20 text-center">
            <h2 className="text-[18px] font-bold">{empty.headline}</h2>
            <p className="max-w-[46ch] text-[14.5px] leading-[23px] text-ink2">{empty.body}</p>
            {empty.cta && (
              <Link
                href={empty.cta.href}
                className="mt-2 rounded-[10px] bg-deep px-5 py-3 text-[14px] font-semibold text-white"
              >
                {empty.cta.label}
```

```bash
"use client";

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

import { CollectionPage } from "@/components/CollectionPage";
import { api } from "@/lib/api";
import type { ListingCard, Me } from "@/lib/types";

/**
 * Saved items — the heart on every card, collected.
 *
 * Sold and reserved listings stay here on purpose. A save outlives the item's
 * availability, and having something quietly disappear because a seller marked
 * it sold reads as data loss rather than as a status change.
 */
export default function SavedPage() {
  const [me, setMe] = useState<Me | null>(null);
  const [items, setItems] = useState<ListingCard[]>([]);
  const [total, setTotal] = useState(0);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    api.me().then(setMe).catch(() => setMe(null));
    api
      .mySaves()
      .then((page) => {
        setItems(page.items);
        setTotal(page.total);
      })
      .catch(() => setTotal(0))
      .finally(() => setLoading(false));
  }, []);

  return (
    <CollectionPage
      me={me}
      title="Saved items"
      blurb="Everything you have tapped the heart on. Saving is private — the seller is never told."
      loading={loading}
      total={total}
      items={items}
      empty={{
        headline: "Nothing saved yet",
        body: "Tap the heart on any listing and it will wait for you here, even after it sells.",
        cta: { href: "/", label: "Browse the feed" },
      }}
    />
  );
}

"use client";
```

```bash
  // keyboard is a trap for anyone not using a mouse.

      if (e.key === "Escape") setOpen(false);

    document.addEventListener("keydown", onKey);
```

**Claude:**

All three pages are built and reachable. **Go look — the avatar menu top-right now opens My listings / Saved items / Inbox / Profile & account / Sign out.**

## What I built

**Backend** — three endpoints that didn't exist (`backend/app/routers/users.py`):

| Endpoint | Returns for `@brian_dw` |
|---|---|
| `GET /me/listings` | 42 — 12 active, 10 sold, 1 reserved, 1 draft |
| `GET /me/saves` | 18, newest save first |
| `GET /me/enquiries` | 7, with channel and seller |

All three reuse `to_card` from the listings router rather than duplicating it, so a card carries identical badges, distance and overlap-only disclosure wherever it appears.

**Frontend** — `/my-listings`, `/saved`, `/inbox`, a shared `CollectionPage` shell, and the avatar menu. Each page has a real empty state with a call to action, since these screens are empty for most members most of the time.

Two fixes the build surfaced:

- **Cards never showed listing status.** The owner couldn't tell a draft from a live post, and §6.4 wants `reserved` marked in the feed too. Status now takes precedence over the condition pill when a listing isn't active — you can see DRAFT, SOLD and RESERVED on My listings.
- **The inbox had two contradictory timestamps** stacked — when you contacted the seller, and when the item was posted. Dropped the second.

I checked Next 16's bundled docs first, as `frontend/AGENTS.md` instructs — `useRouter` from `next/navigation` is still correct, and I avoided `useSearchParams`, which now needs a Suspense boundary.

## Two things worth your attention

**I didn't build `/search`.** Search already works from the nav box on the feed, and a separate route would just duplicate it. What's actually missing is that the nav search box does nothing on other pages — a smaller fix if you want it.

**The photo quality problem is much more visible on these pages.** Saved items shows a car on "Winter boots", couscous on a kitchen item, and — the one I'd genuinely flag — **a photo of an identifiable person as a sofa listing**. Openverse pulls from Flickr, so personal photos come through. Using a stranger's face as a marketplace listing is worse than a wrong object, and it's the strongest argument for switching to Pexels: curated stock, matched subjects, no incidental people. That's the free API key, and it'd be `--source pexels` with everything else unchanged.

Nothing is committed. 24 files modified across `seed/`, `backend/`, `frontend/`, `data/` and the docs.

**Claude:**

Fixed. Nothing was wrong with your scrolling — **there was no pagination anywhere.**

## The bug

The API had always returned `next_cursor`, but no page in the frontend read it. So every list fetched exactly 24 rows and stopped:

| Page | Said | Actually rendered |
|---|---|---|
| Feed | "1,022 items within 2.5 miles" | 24 |
| My listings | "42 items" | 24 |
| Saved items | "18 items" | 18 (under the limit, so it looked fine) |

The header count came from `total`, which is the true number — so the page was telling you there were 1,022 items while showing you 24 of them. Scrolling just hit the end of what had been loaded.

## What I added

Pagination on the feed, My listings and Saved items:

- **Auto-loads as you scroll**, via an `IntersectionObserver` that fires 600px before the end, so items appear before you reach the bottom.
- **A real "Load more" button** underneath as the trigger element, so it works if the observer doesn't — and it's keyboard-reachable, which infinite scroll alone isn't.
- **A progress line**: "Showing 48 of 85", changing to "That is all 42 items." when you reach the end. You now always know whether there's more.
- Appends rather than replaces, and de-duplicates by id so a filter change landing mid-flight can't double up rows.

Verified on My listings: 24 → 42, footer flipping to "That is all 42 items." On the feed: 24 → 48 with "Showing 48 of 85".

**One caveat on what I could verify.** The scroll-triggered auto-load I could *not* test, because the automation tab runs backgrounded and Chrome suspends `IntersectionObserver` for hidden documents — a fresh observer on a visibly in-view element timed out. The button path is proven; the auto-scroll path is standard and should work in your visible window, but it's worth a scroll yourself to confirm.

The inbox is unpaginated on purpose — it fetches 50 and you have 7. Worth revisiting if anyone's inbox gets long.

```
@router.post("/request-link", response_model=LinkSentOut, status_code=status.HTTP_202_ACCEPTED)
def request_link(payload: RequestLinkIn, db: DbSession = Depends(get_db)):
    email = payload.email.lower()
    if not emails.is_allowed(email):
        raise HTTPException(
            status.HTTP_422_UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY,
            emails.rejection_message(),
        )

    user = db.query(User).filter(User.email == email).first()
    if user is None:
        # Deliberately indistinguishable from success: whether an address has an
        # account is not something an unauthenticated caller gets to learn.
        return LinkSentOut(sent=True, resend_available_in_seconds=settings.login_resend_lock_seconds)

    wait = seconds_until_resend(db, user)
    if wait > 0:
        return LinkSentOut(sent=False, resend_available_in_seconds=wait)

    token = issue_login_token(db, user)
    link = _send_link(user, token.token)
    return LinkSentOut(
        sent=True,
        resend_available_in_seconds=settings.login_resend_lock_seconds,
        dev_link=link if settings.email_dev_mode else None,
    )


@router.post("/verify", response_model=MeOut)
def verify(token: str, response: Response, db: DbSession = Depends(get_db)):
```

**Claude:**

`sent: false` doesn't mean failure — it means a link was issued seconds ago and the 60-second resend lock is still on. The page treats it as "show nothing", so the button looks dead. Fixing:


> **`Bash`**

> Fix the dead sign-in button

```bash
cd "/Users/kobeko/Desktop/MBA:MS/Python_bootcamp/secondhand_marketplace" && python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p="frontend/app/signin/page.tsx"; s=open(p, encoding="utf-8").read()

old = '''      const res = await api.requestLink(email);
      setSent(res.sent);
      setDevLink(res.dev_link);
      setWait(res.resend_available_in_seconds);'''
new = '''      const res = await api.requestLink(email);
      // `sent: false` is NOT a failure. It means a link was issued moments ago
      // and the 60-second resend lock (§6.2, state B6) has not expired — the
      // outstanding link is still valid. Treating it as failure left the button
      // looking dead: you clicked, nothing rendered, and the only way to tell a
      // link had been sent was to read the network tab.
      setSent(true);
      setAlreadyPending(!res.sent);
      // Keep any link we already have: a locked resend returns none, but the
      // one from a moment ago still works.
      if (res.dev_link) setDevLink(res.dev_link);
      setWait(res.resend_available_in_seconds);'''
assert old in s
s = s.replace(old, new, 1)

s = s.replace("  const [sent, setSent] = useState(false);",
              "  const [sent, setSent] = useState(false);\n  const [alreadyPending, setAlreadyPending] = useState(false);", 1)

old_box = '''              <p className="text-[16px] font-bold text-deep">Check your Columbia inbox</p>
              <p className="text-[12.5px] leading-[19px] text-ink2">
                The link works once and expires in 15 minutes.
              </p>'''
new_box = '''              <p className="text-[16px] font-bold text-deep">
                {alreadyPending ? "A link is already on its way" : "Check your Columbia inbox"}
              </p>
              <p className="text-[12.5px] leading-[19px] text-ink2">
                {alreadyPending
                  ? "We sent one moments ago — use that one. It works once and expires in 15 minutes."
                  : "The link works once and expires in 15 minutes."}
              </p>'''
assert old_box in s
s = s.replace(old_box, new_box, 1)
open(p, "w", encoding="utf-8").write(s); print("signin fixed")
PYEOF
printf "  /signin HTTP %s\n" "$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://localhost:3000/signin)"
```

**Claude:**

Confirmed — and you were right, there **was** a bug. You're signed in as `@brian_dw` now, on the feed.

## What was wrong

The API returns `sent: false` when you're inside the 60-second resend lock — meaning *"a link went out seconds ago, use that one"*, not *"failed"*. The sign-in page read it as failure:

```js
setSent(res.sent);   // false → the success panel never renders
```

So on a second click within a minute, the button did nothing at all. No panel, no link, no error, no countdown. That's indistinguishable from broken — and it's exactly what you'd hit after logging out, because I'd requested a link for that address moments earlier.

It also silently contradicted UX_SPEC §7 state `B6` ("resend locked, 0:42"), which wants a visible countdown. The countdown existed, but it lived *inside* the panel that never appeared.

## The fix

A successful response now always shows the inbox panel, with the copy distinguishing the two cases — "Check your Columbia inbox" versus "A link is already on its way… we sent one moments ago, use that one." It also keeps the previous dev link on screen rather than blanking it, since that link is still valid.

Verified by driving the real UI: typed the address, clicked the button, got the panel with a clickable link and "Resend available in 0:56", clicked through, landed on the feed signed in.

**One thing worth flagging to Brian:** the same pattern is probably on `/signup`. I only fixed `/signin`, since that's what you hit. Worth a look before anyone demos the sign-up flow twice in a row.

```
/**
 * Turn a FastAPI error body into something a person can read.
 *
 * FastAPI sends two different shapes under `detail`, and only one is a string.
 * A raised HTTPException gives `detail: "That username is taken"`, but a
 * Pydantic validation failure gives an *array* of objects:
 *
 *     [{ type: "value_error", loc: ["body","email"], msg: "Value error, ..." }]
 *
 * Passing that array straight to `new Error()` stringifies it to
 * "[object Object]", so the sign-up form showed exactly that instead of the
 * message naming the four admitted Columbia domains. Same family of bug as the
 * sign-in one: a failure path that renders nothing useful.
 */
function errorMessage(body: unknown, fallback: string): string {
  const detail = (body as { detail?: unknown })?.detail;
  if (typeof detail === "string") return detail;
  if (Array.isArray(detail)) {
    const messages = detail
      .map((d) => (typeof d === "string" ? d : (d as { msg?: string })?.msg))
      .filter(Boolean)
      // Pydantic prefixes its own "Value error, "; the rest is our copy.
      .map((m) => String(m).replace(/^Value error,\s*/, ""));
    if (messages.length) return messages.join(" ");
  }
  return fallback;
}

async function request<T>(path: string, init: RequestInit = {}): Promise<T> {
```

**Claude:**

Checked signup properly, and the answer has two halves.

## The sign-in bug is genuinely not on signup

Signup can't hit it. `POST /auth/signup` always returns `sent: true` on success — there's no resend-lock path, because a repeat attempt raises **409 Conflict** instead. And the page already handles a missing link correctly:

```js
setSent(res.dev_link ?? "sent");   // panel renders either way
```

So I didn't change that. Making a fix there would have been inventing a problem.

## But the same *family* of bug was there, and I did fix it

Testing every signup failure path turned one up. FastAPI sends `detail` in **two different shapes**, and only one is a string:

| Failure | `detail` |
|---|---|
| Duplicate email / username | `"That email already has an account"` — a string |
| ZIP outside metro | `"90210 is not in the New York metro area…"` — a string |
| **Non-Columbia domain** | `[{type, loc, msg}]` — an **array of objects** |

The client did `body.detail ?? res.statusText` and passed it straight to `new Error()`, which stringifies an array of objects to **`[object Object]`**. So entering a Gmail address on signup showed the user literally that, instead of the message naming all four admitted domains.

Same shape of failure as the sign-in one: an error path that renders nothing a person can act on.

The fix is in `frontend/lib/api.ts` — one `errorMessage()` helper that handles both shapes, strips Pydantic's `"Value error, "` prefix, and falls back to the status text. It's in the shared `request()`, so **every** call gets it, not just signup.

Verified against the live API:

```
409 duplicate email  →  "That email already has an account"
422 bad domain       →  "Columbia Market is open to @columbia.edu,
                         @gsb.columbia.edu, @cumc.columbia.edu,
                         @tc.columbia.edu addresses."
```

One caveat on how reachable that was: the signup form validates the email client-side and keeps the submit button disabled, so you'd only hit the raw 422 through a paste-and-submit race or another Pydantic rule firing. It was still wrong, and it's the kind of thing that surfaces exactly when someone's demoing.

> Commit the seed and photo work

```bash
cd "/Users/kobeko/Desktop/MBA:MS/Python_bootcamp/secondhand_marketplace" && git add .gitignore backend/app/services/geo.py backend/scripts/seed.py backend/app/routers/listings.py seed/ scripts/ data/ docs/mock_data_spec.md "frontend/app/listings/[id]/page.tsx" && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG' && git log --oneline -1 | cat
Reconcile the seed data with the backend, and give listings real photos

There were two generators implementing UX_SPEC §9 and they had drifted. The ZIP
tables disagreed — 18 codes in the backend against 47 in seed/ — which put 26%
of generated listings in ZIPs the API rejects, and because geo.zips_within()
resolves the radius filter to a ZIP list, those listings were invisible to every
distance query rather than failing loudly. The backend's grade and school were
also drawn independently, producing undergraduates at CBS, and its saves were
sampled from users who had never viewed the listing, which made any time-based
analysis over saves meaningless.

Now there is one of each:

- backend/app/services/geo.py holds the only ZIP table, extended to 47. seed/
  loads it from there rather than keeping a copy.
- backend/scripts/seed.py is a loader, not a generator. ~360 lines of duplicated
  distributions are gone; the corpus comes from seed/, which owns the
  distributions, the 16-group validator and the §7 state fixtures.
- Emails follow the domain each school issues, so all four admitted domains are
  exercised by the data rather than only by a hand-typed address.

Also fixes the same_zip filter, which compared Listing.zip_code and so let
external listings — a pickup ZIP with no seller behind it — pass a trust filter,
contradicting the paragraph directly above it. It now compares the seller's ZIP,
which is what §5.3 computes the badge from, so the filter and the badge cannot
disagree. On this corpus that had admitted 10 eBay and Facebook rows.

Photos are real now. Each of the ~75 item templates carries its own search
query, filled from the same slot resolution as the title, so "IKEA MALM desk
140×65, white" fetches "white wooden desk" rather than a random desk.
scripts/fetch_photos.py pulls from Openverse (no API key; Pexels and Wikimedia
also supported) and scripts/make_photos.py remains the offline fallback. The
photo URLs are root-relative: a bare "photos/..." resolved against the current
path, so it worked on the feed and 404'd on every detail page.
```

```bash
  GET /me/listings    every status, because drafts and sold items are exactly

  GET /me/saves       newest first; sold and reserved rows stay, since a save

Three bugs found while building them:

1. Nothing paginated. The API had always returned next_cursor and no page read
   it, so the feed announced "1,022 items within 2.5 miles" and rendered 24.
   Scrolling simply ran out. Now the feed and both collections append on scroll,
   with a real Load more button as the trigger element so it works without an
   IntersectionObserver and stays keyboard-reachable, and a "Showing 48 of 85"

2. Cards never showed listing status, so an owner could not tell a draft from a

   Status now takes precedence over the condition pill when a listing is not
   active.

3. Sign-in appeared broken on a second attempt within a minute. `sent: false`

   valid, not that anything failed; the page treated it as failure and rendered
   nothing at all — no panel, no link, no countdown, no error. It now shows the
   inbox panel either way, with copy distinguishing the two cases.

Also flattens FastAPI's two error shapes in one place. A raised HTTPException
gives `detail` as a string, but a Pydantic validation failure gives an array of

sign-up showed the user literally that instead of the message naming all four
```

```
def warn_about_photos() -> None:
    """Say so, loudly, when the photo files the rows point at are not on disk.

    The ~5,800 images are gitignored — they are 200MB and reproducible — so a
    teammate who clones and seeds gets listings whose `url` points at files they
    do not have. The frontend degrades to its gradient placeholder rather than
    breaking, which is worse than an error in one specific way: nothing tells
    you anything is missing. Hence this.
    """
    photos_csv = os.path.join(DATA_DIR, "listing_photos.csv")
    if not os.path.exists(photos_csv):
        return
    with open(photos_csv, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(handle))
    if not rows:
        return

    out_dir = os.path.join(REPO_ROOT, "frontend", "public", "photos")
    # Sample rather than stat 5,800 files.
    sample = rows[:: max(len(rows) // 40, 1)][:40]
    present = sum(
        1 for r in sample
        if os.path.exists(os.path.join(out_dir, r["url"].lstrip("/").split("/", 1)[1]))
    )
    if present >= len(sample):
        return

    share = "none" if present == 0 else "only about %d%%" % round(100 * present / len(sample))
    print("\n" + "!" * 74)
    print("  PHOTOS ARE MISSING — %s of the %d listing photos are on disk."
          % (share, len(rows)))
    print()
    print("  The images are not committed: 200MB, and reproducible from the CSV.")
    print("  The app will still run, showing a gradient placeholder on every card,")
    print("  so this will NOT look like an error. Run this once:")
    print()
    print("      python3 scripts/fetch_photos.py")
    print()
    print("  ~2 minutes, no API key needed. See docs/mock_data_spec.md.")
    print("!" * 74)


def main() -> None:
```

````bash
## What this does

Three commits, reviewable separately.

### `2722292` Reconcile the seed data with the backend, and give listings real photos

There were **two generators** implementing UX_SPEC §9 and they had drifted:

| | backend | `seed/` |
|---|---|---|
| ZIP table | 18 codes | 47 codes |
| grade × school | drawn independently → undergraduates at CBS | conditional |
| saves | sampled from users who never viewed the listing | derived from an actual view |

The ZIP split was the damaging one: **26% of generated listings sat in ZIPs the API rejects**, and because `geo.zips_within()` resolves the radius filter to a ZIP list, those listings were invisible to every distance query rather than failing loudly.

Now there is one of each. `backend/app/services/geo.py` holds the only ZIP table (extended to 47); `seed/zips.py` loads it from there. `backend/scripts/seed.py` is a **loader**, not a generator — ~360 lines of duplicated distributions removed. Emails follow the domain each school issues, so all four admitted domains are exercised by data rather than by a hand-typed address.

**Also fixes `same_zip`**, which compared `Listing.zip_code` and so let external listings — a pickup ZIP with no seller behind it — pass a trust filter, contradicting the comment directly above it. It now compares the seller's ZIP, which is what §5.3 computes the badge from. On this corpus that had admitted 10 eBay and Facebook rows into a trust-filtered feed.

**Photos** are matched to each item. Every one of the ~75 templates carries its own search query, filled from the same slot resolution as the title — so `IKEA MALM desk 140×65, white` fetches *white wooden desk*, not a random desk.
````

**3. `data/README.md`** leads with it.

The key insight worth stating plainly: the failure mode here is *worse than an error*. A missing image that 404s is obvious; a gradient placeholder that was designed to look good is invisible. Anyone would assume that's just how it looks.

```
# One command to run the MVP locally: API on :8000, app on :3000.

PY=backend/.venv/bin/python

    uv pip install --python "$PY" -r backend/requirements.txt
  else
    python3.12 -m venv backend/.venv

  fi

[ -f backend/.env ] || cp backend/.env.example backend/.env

cleanup() { kill 0 2>/dev/null || true; }
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

(cd frontend && exec npm run dev) &
```

**It's running.** Switch to the Chrome tab — API on `localhost:8000`, app on `localhost:3000`, signed in as `@brian_dw`, 85 items, photos loading.

You can also see PR #9's addition, which he didn't mention: a "Filtering by · Same nationality ✕ · Clear all" chip row and "First 24 of 85 shown — scroll for the rest".

## Reading his message carefully — three things worth knowing

**1. "pull the latest in main" needed a `--reseed`, and `dev.sh` wouldn't have done it.** Your local database was from the old schema. `dev.sh` only seeds when `backend/columbia_market.db` is *absent*, so it would have started against a stale DB and looked broken. I deleted it first, so it seeded clean. **Tell the others to run `./dev.sh --reseed`, not plain `./dev.sh`** — anyone who ran the app before today hits this.

**2. His "1,350 listings" is correct but worth understanding.** He dropped the external tier — the schema has no `source` column since `docs/DECISIONS.md`. So the loader skips 150 of my rows on the way in and says so:

```
listings.csv   1350 rows
                150 rows skipped — external tier, not in the schema
```

My generator still emits them. Not a bug, but the two-tier feed from the proposal is now out of scope, which is a real product decision worth confirming everyone knows.

**3. `dev.sh` half-failed on your machine, and it's the colon again.** The API came up fine; the frontend died:

```
sh: next: command not found
```

`npm run dev` puts `node_modules/.bin` on `PATH`, which splits at `MBA:MS`. I started it with `./node_modules/.bin/next dev` instead. **This will happen every time you run `dev.sh`** — it's specific to your folder name, not the repo. Renaming `MBA:MS` to `MBA-MS` fixes it permanently and makes `dev.sh` work as written.

Two smaller things: I deleted your `frontend/.env.local` (it pointed at 8001 from when Wordcraft held 8000 — Wordcraft is stopped now, so the default 8000 is right), and all 5,786 photos were already on disk so no fetch was needed.

The platform **runs without errors today.** 61/61 backend tests pass, TypeScript is clean, no frontend errors, and the analytics layer runs end to end against the seeded corpus. The API's only non-2xx are correct behaviour — 401s on signed-out `/me`, one 400 on a deliberately reused single-use token.

So the missing pieces are features and hardening, not breakage. Here's what's actually absent, ordered by whether it blocks something:

## Broken links — things the UI points at that don't exist

The mobile tab bar links to **`/search`** and **`/inbox`**. `/inbox` I built, but `/search` still 404s. That's the only genuine dead end in the product right now, and it's the cheapest thing on this list — search already works from the nav box on the feed, so it needs a route that reads `?q=` rather than new logic.

## Screens and states from the spec, unbuilt

- The **mobile filter sheet** (`C10`) — filters are desktop-sidebar only
- The **photo lightbox** (`D2`)
- The **price histogram** in the price filter (`C8`)
- **Drafts** — the status exists in the schema and my seed data has draft rows, but there's no way to create or edit one
- Most of the remaining §7 interaction states

## Infrastructure, before this leaves a laptop

- **Alembic.** The schema is created with `create_all()`, so every change means dropping the database. Vinayak flags this himself — it should land before the schema stabilises, not after.
- **Postgres and object storage.** SQLite and local disk work for the demo; neither survives deployment.
- **Rate limiting** beyond the resend lock and the hourly enquiry cap.
- **A terms page**, which the sign-up consent checkbox needs — and that checkbox is what covers research use of the behavioural data, so it matters for the analysis being publishable.

## For the coursework specifically

Two things stand out more than the frontend gaps:

**The badge experiment is off.** Q1 reports one arm only — 63,567 impressions all treated, no control. It's instrumented but `BADGE_EXPERIMENT_ENABLED` defaults to false, so the single genuinely causal result in the proposal has no data. That's a one-line env change, but every impression logged until it's flipped is unusable for that question.

**The analysis runs on my generated data**, which means anything it finds is a test of the pipeline, not a result. Q2 and Q3 are the exception — filter depth and toggle behaviour are structural, so those numbers are meaningful. Q1's badge effect and any in-group price discount are not, by construction: §9 told me not to plant them and I didn't.

**Still unresolved as a product question:** the name. UI and API say "Columbia Market", the repo and course say "LionsList". Worth settling before slides get made.

I've dug into this and there's something important to say before the questions: **most of what you're describing already exists.** I generated four behavioural tables back in the seed work, and they're live in the database right now:

| Table | Rows | What it captures |
|---|---:|---|

And `backend/app/analytics/questions.py` already answers five research questions in pandas against them. I ran it just now; it works.

So both your examples are **already answerable**: "how many items listed this week" is a `posted_at` resample, and the seasonality chart exists.

## But your second example exposes the real gap

**"How many items were sold within 2.5 miles"** — you *can't* answer that today. `sold_at` records that a sale happened, but **there's no buyer on it.** Distance is always computed viewer-to-listing, so "within 2.5 miles" has no second endpoint once the sale is done. That's the single biggest hole, and it's exactly the question you reached for.

Alongside it: there's no `session_id` (so funnels are approximated), no search-query log (so "what are people searching for" is unanswerable), no unsave events, and no status history (a listing goes active → reserved → sold but only the end state survives).

Also worth knowing: **the badge experiment is running one-armed.** `badges_shown` is on every one of the 63,567 impressions, so the one genuinely causal question in the proposal has no control group.

Four things I need from you before building:

**Claude:**

Good question — and yes, `buyer_id` doesn't populate itself. Here's what it needs.

## The UI it requires: one step in a flow that already exists

Today "mark as sold" is a single seller action (`POST /listings/{id}/sold`). To capture a buyer you add one screen to it:

> **Who bought it?**
> — a list of the people who enquired about this listing (you already have `enquiries.buyer_id`, so the candidates are known)
> — plus **"Someone else"** and **"Sold outside Columbia Market"**

That's the whole feature. It's low friction because the seller picks from 2–5 names rather than searching, and it's what Karrot and Facebook Marketplace both do. No new disclosure problem either — the seller already knows who contacted them.

**`buyer_id` must stay nullable.** Plenty of real sales go to a friend, or to someone who never enquired. That's not a defect — *"what share of sales are attributable to an in-app enquiry"* is itself one of your better charts, and you only get it if the null case is representable.

## One thing I'd add alongside it

**`sold_price_cents`**, also nullable. If a seller edits the price after listing, the original `price_cents` is overwritten and the actual sale price is lost — which quietly breaks the in-group discount analysis, one of the proposal's five questions. It's a second small column and it closes most of the gap between your option 2 and a full transactions table.

With those two columns plus the mark-sold step, option 2 gets you:

- sale distance (buyer ZIP ↔ listing ZIP) — your original question
- in-group vs out-group sales (did they share school / nationality / ZIP)
- enquiry → purchase conversion, since buyers are picked from enquirers
- repeat buyers and repeat sellers
- actual sale price vs asking price

What you'd still lack versus a transactions table: relist history (an item sold, returned, sold again) and a clean record if a listing is edited heavily. Both are minor at this scale.

## Two flags before I start

**The dashboard choice has a syllabus risk.** You picked the in-app dashboard, and the syllabus says the analysis component "should involve some amount of Python." So the aggregation needs to live in Python — FastAPI endpoints doing the pandas work, with TypeScript only drawing the charts. That satisfies it, but if the grader looks for a visible Python artefact, a dashboard alone is thinner evidence than a notebook. Worth deciding deliberately rather than by default.

**Schema changes are Jae and Vinayak's territory.** `buyer_id`, `sold_price_cents`, `session_id` on four tables, and a new search-events table all touch `models.py` — and there's no Alembic yet, so every change means dropping and reseeding the database. Worth a message before I write it, not after.

Confirm two things and I'll start:

2. **Have you cleared the schema changes with Jae and Vinayak**, or should I keep everything additive and nullable so their code can ignore it entirely?

## 48. Kobe — 2026-09-03 13:30

1. yes, 2. What do you mean by keep everything additive and nullable?


**Claude:**

"Additive and nullable" means writing the schema change so that **nobody else's code has to change at all.**

## Additive

Only *add* things. Never rename, remove, retype, or tighten anything that exists.

| Additive — safe | Not additive — breaks people |
|---|---|
| Add `buyer_id` (nullable) to `listings` | Rename `sold_at` → `sold_on` |
| Add a new `search_events` table | Drop the `view_count` column |
| Add `session_id` to `listing_views` | Change `price_cents` int → decimal |
| | Add `NOT NULL` with no default |
| | Add a UNIQUE constraint existing rows violate |

Everything in the left column is invisible to code that doesn't know about it. Everything on the right makes Jae's and Vinayak's code fail on the next run.

## Nullable

The new columns permit `NULL` and require no value. That matters because their existing write paths don't know these fields exist:

```python
# Vinayak's mark-sold endpoint, unchanged:
listing.status = ListingStatus.SOLD
listing.sold_at = now()
# buyer_id and sold_price_cents simply stay NULL — no error
```

If I made `buyer_id` `NOT NULL`, that endpoint would crash on every sale until he updated it. Nullable means his code keeps working, and mine fills the columns in where it can.

It's also honest modelling, not just defensive: a sale genuinely might have no in-app buyer, so `NULL` carries real meaning — *"sold, but not to anyone we can identify."*

## The one thing nullable does *not* save you from

**There's no Alembic.** The schema is built by `create_all()`, which creates *missing tables* but will **not** add a column to a table that already exists. So an existing `columbia_market.db` won't pick up `buyer_id` — it'll keep the old shape and then error when the code selects a column SQLite doesn't have.

Practical consequence: **everyone has to reseed once.**

```bash
cd backend && .venv/bin/python -m scripts.seed --reset
```

They already do that after pulling data changes, so it's one line in your message, not a crisis. But it's why this needs a heads-up before it lands, not after — anyone who pulls and doesn't reseed sees a confusing `no such column` error.

---

So the answer to your question 2 is: **I'll keep it additive and nullable regardless.** It's the right call here whether or not you've spoken to them — it means the only thing they have to do is reseed, and nothing they've written stops working.

What I'd still send them, before I push: *"adding 2 nullable columns to listings, a session_id to the four event tables, and a search_events table — all additive, but you'll need `--reset` once."*

Ready to start. I'll do it in this order: schema first, then regenerate the seed data to populate it, then the mark-sold buyer step, then the dashboard.

```
def generate_events(rng, users, listings, photos, now):
    """Return ``(listing_views, saves, enquiries, filter_events)``.

    Counters on the listing rows are updated in place, so after this call
    ``view_count`` equals the number of ``listing_views`` rows referencing it.
    """
    photo_counts: "dict[str, int]" = {}
    for photo in photos:
        photo_counts[photo["listing_id"]] = photo_counts.get(photo["listing_id"], 0) + 1

    users_by_id = {u["id"]: u for u in users}
    viewers = [u for u in users if u["is_verified"]]
    viewers.sort(key=lambda u: u["created_at"])
    joined = [u["created_at"] for u in viewers]

    views: "list[dict]" = []
    saves: "list[dict]" = []
    enquiries: "list[dict]" = []
    saved_pairs: "set[tuple[str, str]]" = set()

    for listing in listings:
        # §4.5: a draft was never published, so nobody has seen it.
        if listing["status"] == "draft":
            continue

        photo_count = photo_counts.get(listing["id"], 1)
        target = int(round(_expected_views(rng, listing, photo_count, now)))
        window_end = min(listing["sold_at"] or now, now)
        window = (window_end - listing["posted_at"]).total_seconds()
        if window <= 0:
            continue

        seller_id = listing["seller_id"]
        seller = users_by_id.get(seller_id) if seller_id else None

        for _ in range(target):
            # Views cluster early in a listing's life; sqrt biases towards the
            # first days without excluding the tail.
            at = listing["posted_at"] + dt.timedelta(
                seconds=window * (rng.random() ** 2)
            )
            if at > now:

            # §6.2: "There is no browsing without an account in the pilot", so a
            # viewer is always attributable. The column stays nullable because a
            # deactivated account's rows outlive its profile.
            limit = bisect.bisect_right(joined, at)
```

```bash
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Sessions, searches and buyers  (added 2026-09-03)
#
# Three passes that run after the event tables exist, because each one needs
# them: a session is a grouping of events, a search is compared against the
# corpus, and a buyer is chosen from the people who enquired.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def sessionise(views, saves, enquiries, filter_events, searches):
    """Group every event into visits and stamp a `session_id` on each.

    Definition: one person's events, split wherever they go quiet for
    SESSION_GAP_MINUTES. That is the same rule Google Analytics uses, and it is
    chosen deliberately over inventing a session at generation time — the events
    were produced independently, so grouping them afterwards is both simpler and
    closer to how a real pipeline would derive sessions from a raw log.

    Returns the number of sessions created.
    """
    streams = (
        (views, "viewer_id", "viewed_at"),
        (saves, "user_id", "created_at"),
        (enquiries, "buyer_id", "created_at"),
        (filter_events, "user_id", "created_at"),
        (searches, "user_id", "created_at"),
    )

    by_user: "dict[str, list]" = {}
    for rows, user_key, time_key in streams:
        for row in rows:
            user = row.get(user_key)
            if user is None:
                row["session_id"] = None
                continue
            by_user.setdefault(user, []).append((row[time_key], row))

    gap = dt.timedelta(minutes=SESSION_GAP_MINUTES)
    sessions = 0
    for user, events in by_user.items():
        events.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[0])
        current = None
        previous = None
        for when, row in events:
            if previous is None or (when - previous) > gap:
                # A session id derived from the user and the visit's first
                # timestamp, so it is stable across regenerations.
                current = str(uuid.uuid5(
                    uuid.NAMESPACE_URL, "%s:%s" % (user, when.isoformat())))
                sessions += 1
            row["session_id"] = current
            previous = when
    return sessions
```

```bash
def cluster_into_visits(rng, users, listings, views, saves, enquiries,
                        filter_events, searches, now):

    Events are generated independently — a view is drawn from its listing's own
    lifetime — so a person's activity ends up scattered across two years and
    every event lands in a session of one. Real browsing is bursty: you open the
    app, look at eight things, and leave.

    So each member gets a set of visit timestamps, and every event of theirs is
    snapped to the nearest visit that is *legal for that event* — a view cannot
    move outside the window in which its listing was actually on the feed. When
    no visit fits, the event keeps its own time and becomes a session of one,
    which is a real pattern too.

    This changes timestamps by hours, never by which day-of-week or season they
```

**Claude:**

The data layer is done. **61/61 tests still pass**, which is the proof it stayed additive — none of Jae's or Vinayak's code needed touching.

## What's now in the database

| | |
|---|---|
| **Buyers on sales** | 323 of 452 sales have an identified buyer (71%); the rest are NULL, meaning sold to someone who never enquired |
| **Sale prices** | `sold_price_cents` captured separately, so a later price edit can't destroy it |
| **Sessions** | 17,141 visits — median 2 events, p90 11, max 54 |
| **Searches** | 2,774 queries, **907 returned nothing** |
| **Badge experiment** | 50/50 arms — 28,760 control vs 28,804 treated |

Your original question is now answerable: 323 sales have both parties known, so sale distance, in-group vs out-group trade and repeat buyers are all computable.

**The badge experiment has a result for the first time:**

```
badges hidden   28,760 impressions   637 contacts   2.21%
badges shown    28,804 impressions   777 contacts   2.70%
lift p-value: 0.0002
```

That's the planted 1.35× lift being recovered — which is exactly what it should do, and exactly what the write-up must say it is.

## Two things I changed that go beyond "just data"

**A purchase now implies contact.** Only 15% of sales had a buyer at first, because enquiries are drawn per-view at a flat rate with no knowledge of who bought. Rather than leave sales unattributed, I add the missing enquiry — buying without ever contacting the seller isn't a path this product has. Enquiries rose 824 → 1,079 as a result.

**Events are clustered into visits.** Generated independently, each person's activity was scattered across two years and every session had one event. Members now get visit timestamps and events snap to the nearest *legal* one — a view can't move outside the window its listing was actually on the feed.

**Every planted effect is declared in one block** at the top of `seed/events.py`: badge lift 1.35×, overlap engagement 1.18× per shared attribute, distance decay 3.5mi, in-group discount 4% per shared attribute, 72% buyer attribution. The rule I used: if a reader could mistake the chart for evidence about the real world, it must be listed.

## What's left

Three things, in order:

1. **The mark-sold buyer step** — the UI that populates `buyer_id` from real usage, not just seed data
2. **The dashboard** — Python aggregation endpoints, TypeScript charts
3. **`docs/mock_data_spec.md`** — the planted-effects section, which matters most for the write-up

Nothing is committed yet. Worth telling Jae and Vinayak now, before I go further: *2 nullable columns on listings, session_id on four event tables, one new search_events table — all additive, but everyone needs `--reset` once.*

```
function OwnerActions({
  listing,
  onChange,
}: {
  listing: ListingDetail;
  onChange: (l: ListingDetail) => void;
}) {
  const [busy, setBusy] = useState(false);
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);

  async function set(status: ListingStatus) {
    setBusy(true);
    setError(null);
    try {
      onChange(await api.updateListing(listing.id, { status }));
    } catch (e) {
      setError(e instanceof Error ? e.message : "Could not update the listing");
    } finally {
      setBusy(false);
    }
  }

  const s = listing.status;
  return (
    <div className="flex flex-col gap-3">
      <SectionLabel>YOUR LISTING</SectionLabel>
      <p className="text-[12.5px] leading-[18px] text-ink2">
        Buyers see this page without these controls. Marking it sold keeps the page reachable but
        removes it from every feed.
      </p>
      <div className="flex flex-wrap gap-2">
        {s !== "sold" && (
          <Button disabled={busy} onClick={() => set("sold")}>
            Mark as sold
          </Button>
        )}
        {s === "active" && (
          <Button variant="ghost" disabled={busy} onClick={() => set("reserved")}>
            Mark reserved
          </Button>
        )}
        {s !== "active" && (
          <Button variant="ghost" disabled={busy} onClick={() => set("active")}>
            {s === "sold" ? "Relist" : "Put back on sale"}
          </Button>
        )}
        {s !== "delisted" && (
          <Button variant="danger" disabled={busy} onClick={() => set("delisted")}>
            Take down
          </Button>
        )}
      </div>
      {error && <p className="text-[12px] text-danger">{error}</p>}
    </div>
  );
}

/**
 * Overlap-only disclosure made visible — UX_SPEC.md §5.3.
 *
 * The item, the price and the photos are identical for every viewer. Only this
 * block changes.
```

```
# Data & visualisation spec

**Owner:** Kobe · **Scope:** the behavioural ("user action") data and what can be
built on it · **Companion to:** [`mock_data_spec.md`](mock_data_spec.md), which
covers users, listings and photos.

> **If you are about to plot something from this data, read §6 first.** Several of
> the effects the charts will show were put there deliberately. Which ones, and
> how large, is written down — but a chart made without knowing that is a chart
> that claims more than it can.

---

## 1. What this covers

`mock_data_spec.md` describes the *content* of the marketplace — who the members
are and what they listed. This document describes what those members **did**:
every impression, save, contact, filter toggle, search and completed sale, and
how each was generated.

The syllabus asks for a data-analysis component involving Python. This is the
data that component runs on.

### Current volume

| Table | Rows | One row is |
|---|---:|---|
| `listing_views` | 64,020 | one listing shown to one person |
| `saves` | 6,105 | tapping the heart |
| `enquiries` | 1,079 | revealing a seller's contact details |
| `filter_events` | 3,129 | one filter toggle or slider release |
| `search_events` | 2,774 | one typed query |
| `listings` (sold) | 454 | a completed sale, 324 with an identified buyer |
| — sessions | 17,141 | one browsing visit, mean 3.7 events |

Roughly 77,000 behavioural rows over a two-year window (Aug 2024 → Sep 2026).

---

## 2. The event model

Five streams, each answering something the others cannot.

### `listing_views` — impressions

`id`, `listing_id`, `viewer_id`, `surface`, `badges_shown`, `viewed_at`, `session_id`

The top of every funnel. `surface` distinguishes feed / search / detail, so
browsing and searching can be compared. `badges_shown` carries the experiment's
coin flip — see §5.

Views cluster early in a listing's life (a square-law bias towards the first
days), scale with age, photo count and price, and are **blind to whether the
listing is any good** — there is no quality score putting a thumb on the scale.

### `saves` — private interest

`id`, `listing_id`, `user_id`, `created_at`, `session_id`

Drawn from a view that happened, at ~8% — never sampled independently, so every
save has a real impression behind it. Unique on `(user, listing)`.

### `enquiries` — the contact reveal

`id`, `listing_id`, `buyer_id`, `channel`, `created_at`, `session_id`

The strongest intent signal short of a sale, and the moment the se
```

- **§4** — buyers and prices, and why `NULL` is data rather than absence
- **§6** — **the planted effects table.** Every parameter, its value, and why it exists — alongside what is *not* planted (search result counts, `filter_events.result_count`, time-to-sale). With the line I'd want in the write-up: a chart of the badge lift is a test that the pipeline works, not a finding about Columbia students.
- **§7** — about 25 concrete visualisations grouped by axis, all computable today
- **§9** — what still can't be asked: no unsaves, no status history, no price-change path, no feed position

The structural ones — filter-depth inventory, the 33% empty-search rate, funnel drop-off — genuinely can. ## 51. Kobe — 2026-09-03 13:51

I dont understand your point on $6. Can you explain it me more easily?


**Claude:**

Sure — here it is without the jargon.

## The problem in one sentence

I wrote the program that created the fake data. So when the analysis "discovers" something, it's often just reading back an instruction I typed.

## A concrete example

In `seed/events.py` I wrote a line that effectively says:

> *"When someone sees match badges, make them 1.35× more likely to contact the seller."*

Then the analysis ran and reported:

```
badges hidden   2.21% contact rate
badges shown    2.70% contact rate     ← 2.70 / 2.21 ≈ 1.22×
p-value: 0.0002
```

That looks like a finding. It isn't. It's my own number coming back to me, slightly blurred by randomness. The tiny p-value just means I generated enough rows.

It's like hiding an Easter egg in your garden, then announcing you found an Easter egg in your garden. True, but not news.

## But not everything is like that

Some numbers I genuinely didn't choose. Take this one:

> **33% of searches return zero results.**

I picked the list of words people search for, and separately the templates that generate listing titles. I never wrote "make a third of searches fail." The computer actually matched each query against the real titles and counted. That 33% *emerged* — it tells you something true about how well the catalogue covers what people look for.

Same for how many listings survive each filter, and where people drop out of the funnel. Those come from running the real query over the real corpus, not from a number I set.

## So the two piles

| I set this — it's a **demo** | It emerged — it's a **result** |
|---|---|
| Badges lift contact by 1.35× | 33% of searches find nothing |
| In-group discount of 4% | How many listings survive each filter |
| Seasonality spike of 3× | Drop-off between funnel stages |
| 72% of sales have a known buyer | Time-to-sale distribution |

## What this means for your report

Both piles are worth showing — they're the same charts either way. The difference is only in the sentence underneath:

- Left pile: *"This chart demonstrates our pipeline can detect a badge effect if one exists."*
- Right pile: *"A third of searches return nothing, which tells us what the catalogue is missing."*

The right-hand pile is stronger material, because it says something even though the data is synthetic. If I'd hidden the planted numbers instead of listing them, someone could have written "we found that badges increase contact by 22%" — and that would have been wrong in a way that's hard to catch later.

That's all §6 is: the list of which pile each number belongs in.

> **`Bash`**

> Commit the behavioural data layer

```bash
cd "/Users/kobeko/Desktop/MBA:MS/Python_bootcamp/secondhand_marketplace" && git checkout -b feat/action-data 2>&1 | tail -1 && git add backend/app/models.py backend/scripts/seed.py seed/ data/ && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG' && git log --oneline -1 | cat
Record what members actually did: sessions, searches, buyers and sale prices

The corpus described who was on the marketplace and what they listed. It said
much less about what people did with it, and three gaps made whole questions
unanswerable.

A sale had only a date. "How many items sold within 2.5 miles" has no second
endpoint without knowing who bought it, so `listings` gains `buyer_id` and
`sold_price_cents`. Both nullable, because a sale to a friend or off-platform is
real and common — 71% of sales now have an identified buyer and the other 29%
are a figure worth charting rather than missing data. `sold_price_cents` is
separate from `price_cents` because a seller editing a listing overwrites the
asking price and takes the in-group discount question with it.

A buyer is drawn from the people who enquired before the sale, which is what
makes enquiry-to-purchase conversion a measurement rather than a coincidence.
Where a listing sold with no prior enquiry the enquiry is added rather than the
sale left unattributed: buying without contacting the seller is not a path this
product has. Enquiries rose 824 -> 1,079 for that reason.

Every event was its own session. Events are generated independently — a view is
drawn from its listing's lifetime — so a person's activity scattered across two
years and the funnel could only be approximated with a time window. Members now
get visit timestamps derived from how much they actually did, each event snaps
to the nearest visit that is *legal for it* (a view cannot move outside the
window its listing was on the feed), and sessions come from the standard
30-minute inactivity gap. 17,141 sessions, mean 3.7 events, median 2.

Free-text search was not recorded at all. `search_events` captures the query,
how many results came back and whether it led to a click. Result counts are real
substring matches against live titles, so the 33% of searches that return
nothing is measured rather than set — one of the few numbers here that says
something even though the corpus is synthetic.

The badge experiment now has two arms. The loader hardcoded `badges_shown=True`
```

```bash
Ask who bought it when a seller marks something sold

Seed data recording buyers is worth little if real usage cannot produce the same
rows, so the mark-sold flow now captures one.

GET /listings/{id}/enquirers lists the people who have contacted the seller.
Owner only, and no new disclosure: they already received those enquiries, so
this says nothing their inbox does not.

POST /listings/{id}/sold takes an optional {buyer_id, sold_price_cents}. The
body and every field in it are optional, so the no-body call that existed before
behaves exactly as it did. The API refuses a buyer who never enquired and
refuses self-purchase — you cannot sell to someone who never contacted you
through the app, and allowing it would quietly break the conversion figures.
Sale price falls back to the asking price: the seller marked it sold, so that is
what it went for unless they said otherwise.

The UI adds one step to the owner controls rather than a new screen: "Who bought
it?" listing each enquirer with how and when they got in touch, plus "Sold to
someone else" for the friend-or-off-platform case, which records the sale with a
null buyer. Fetching the list is best-effort — if it fails the seller can still
mark the item sold, because recording the buyer is worth having and not worth
blocking a sale over.

docs/data_visualization_spec.md covers the behavioural data end to end: the five
event streams and what each uniquely answers, how sessions are derived, the
buyer and price model, and roughly 25 visualisations the tables now support. Its
§6 lists every planted effect and its value beside what is genuinely emergent,
so a chart is never mistaken for a finding it cannot support.
```

````bash
---

## Why

The corpus said who was on the marketplace and what they listed. It said very little about what people *did*, and three gaps made whole questions unanswerable.

### A sale had only a date

"How many items sold within 2.5 miles" has no second endpoint without a buyer. `listings` gains `buyer_id` and `sold_price_cents`, both nullable — a sale to a friend or off-platform is real and common, so **71% of sales now have an identified buyer** and the other 29% is a figure worth charting rather than missing data.

`sold_price_cents` is separate from `price_cents` because editing a listing overwrites the asking price and takes the in-group discount question with it.

A buyer is drawn from people who **enquired before the sale**, which makes enquiry-to-purchase conversion a measurement rather than a coincidence. Where something sold with no prior enquiry, the enquiry is added rather than the sale left unattributed — buying without contacting the seller is not a path this product has. That is why enquiries rose 824 → 1,079.

### Every event was its own session

Events are generated independently, so a person's activity scattered across two years and every session held one event. Members now get visit timestamps derived from how much they actually did; each event snaps to the nearest visit **that is legal for it** — a view cannot move outside the window its listing was on the feed. Sessions then come from the standard 30-minute inactivity gap.

**17,141 sessions, mean 3.7 events, median 2, p90 11.**

### Search was not recorded at all

`search_events` captures the query, the result count and whether it led to a click. Counts are real substring matches against live titles, so the **33% of searches that return nothing is measured, not set** — one of the few numbers that says something even though the corpus
… [2,049 more characters]
````

```
"""Aggregates for the dashboard — the analysis component, in Python.

Every figure the /insights page draws is computed here with pandas and handed to
the client as plain numbers. The frontend draws; it does not analyse. That split
is deliberate: the coursework asks for the data analysis to be Python, and it
also keeps one definition of "a sale" or "a session" rather than one per chart.

Aggregation is done with SQL `GROUP BY` feeding small DataFrames, not by loading
64,000 view rows into memory on every request. `app/analytics/frames.py` remains
the place for exploratory work in a notebook, where loading everything is the
point.

Read `docs/data_visualization_spec.md` §6 before presenting any of this: several
of the effects visible here were planted in the seed data and are listed there.
"""

          (select count(*) from listings where status = 'active')         as active,
          (select count(*) from listing_views)                            as views,
          (select count(*) from saves)                                    as saves,
          (select count(*) from enquiries)                                as enquiries,
          (select count(distinct session_id) from listing_views
             where session_id is not null)                                as sessions,
          (select count(*) from search_events)                            as searches
    """)
    row = df.iloc[0]
    return {k: int(row[k]) for k in df.columns}
```

```
"use client";

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

import { MobileTabBar, TopNav } from "@/components/TopNav";
import { Card, SectionLabel } from "@/components/ui";
import { api } from "@/lib/api";
import type { Insights, Me } from "@/lib/types";

/**
 * Dashboard — UX_SPEC has no screen for this; it exists for the coursework's
 * data-analysis component.
 *
 * Every number here is computed in Python (`backend/app/routers/insights.py`)
 * with pandas and arrives as plain values. This file draws; it does not
 * analyse. Charts are hand-drawn SVG rather than a charting library, so the
 * project gains no dependency for six charts.
 *
 * On reading these figures: several of the effects visible here were planted in
 * the seed data, and which ones is listed in docs/data_visualization_spec.md §6.
 * The badge panel says so on the page itself, because that is the one a reader
 * is most likely to mistake for a finding.
 */
export default function InsightsPage() {
  const [me, setMe] = useState<Me | null>(null);
  const [data, setData] = useState<Insights | null>(null);
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    api.me().then(setMe).catch(() => setMe(null));
    api
      .insights()
      .then(setData)
      .catch((e) => setError(e instanceof Error ? e.message : "Could not load"));
  }, []);

  return (
    <>
      <TopNav me={me} />
      <main className="mx-auto max-w-[1360px] px-4 py-7 pb-24 md:px-10 md:pb-10">
        <header className="mb-7 flex flex-col gap-1.5">
          <h1 className="text-[26px] font-bold tracking-[-0.02em] md:text-[32px]">Dashboard</h1>
          <p className="max-w-[70ch] text-[14.5px] leading-[23px] text-ink2">
            What is on the marketplace and what people do with it. Every figure is
            aggregated in Python from the event tables — impressions, saves, contacts,
            searches and completed sales.
          </p>
        </header>

        {error && <p className="text-[14px] text-danger">{error}</p>}
        {!data && !error && <p className="py-20 text-center text-ink2">Loading…</p>}

        {data && (
          <div className="flex flex-col gap-6">
            <Overview data={data} />

            <div className="grid gap-6 lg:grid-cols-2">
              <Activity data={data} />
              <Funnel data={data} />
              <Distance data={data} />
              <Searches data={data} />
            </div>

            <Categories data={data} />
… [10,500 more characters]
```

**Claude:**

The dashboard is live — **http://localhost:3000/insights**, reachable from the **Dashboard** item in the avatar menu (top-right) and the mobile tab bar.

## What's there

Seven panels, all from real seeded behaviour:

- **Headline tiles** — 1,000 members, 1,350 listings, 64,068 views, 17,141 visits
- **Weekly posted vs sold** — the May/August move-out spikes are clearly visible
- **Funnel** — views → saves (9.5%) → enquiries (17.7%) → sales (41.9%)
- **Sale distance** — your original question: 102 same-ZIP, 51 within a mile, 88 within 2.5, and 129 with no identified buyer shown rather than hidden
- **Searches** — with the empty ones flagged in amber
- **Categories** — volume, sell-through, median price
- **Badge experiment** — both arms

## The architecture, for the syllabus

The analysis is genuinely Python. `backend/app/routers/insights.py` does every aggregation with pandas and returns plain numbers; the page only draws. Charts are hand-written SVG, so the project gained **no new dependency** for six charts.

## One thing the dashboard immediately surfaced

Look at the search panel: **`textbook` — 82 searches, 82 empty. `office chair` — 79 searches, 79 empty.** Those return nothing while `vacuum` and `rice cooker` convert fine.

That's not a planted effect — it's my search-term list not matching how titles are actually generated. Titles say *"Corporate Finance (Berk) 5th ed."*, never the word "textbook"; and *"HON Ignition, size C"*, never "office chair". So a real gap in the catalogue's searchability showed up the moment it was plotted, which is the dashboard doing its job.

Worth fixing — either titles should carry the generic noun, or search should match category names too. Your call whether that's a data fix or a backend one.

Nothing committed. Want me to commit this, and shall I look at the search-matching gap?

**Claude:**

The top-line section is live. Day / Week / Month all switch instantly, and the May and August spikes are unmistakable in the monthly view.

## What it shows

Eight tiles, each with **period-over-period change**, plus a grouped bar chart of listed vs sold at the chosen granularity. The comparison deliberately excludes the bucket in progress — a half-finished week always looks like a collapse.

## The missing top-lines you asked about — I added five

You mentioned listed and sold. Here's what else the data already supports, and why each earns a place:

| Metric | Why it belongs |
|---|---|
| **Value sold (GMV)** | The single most standard marketplace top-line. Two items at $400 is not the same week as twenty at $15, and a count alone can't tell you which happened. Uses `sold_price_cents`. |
| **Sell-through** | Sold ÷ listed. Catches the failure mode where listings climb and sales don't — supply growing faster than demand. |
| **New members** | Growth, separated from activity. |
| **Active members** | Distinct people who viewed anything. This is what stops every other number being misread: listings up 160% looks like a triumph until you see active members only rose 17.5%. |
| **Contacts** | Real buying intent. Views are cheap; contacting a stranger isn't. |
| **Searches** | Demand people express in their own words, and the source of the empty-search signal. |

Two more are computed and returned but not tiled yet, if you want them: **sellers** and **buyers** (distinct people on each side, which gives you concentration — are 200 listings coming from 20 sellers or 150?), and **contact rate** (contacts ÷ views).

## One thing worth naming

Look at the week view: **Contacts −17.1% while everything else rose.** Listings +8.2%, value sold +86.4%, searches +119%. That's the kind of divergence a top-line exists to surface — more supply and more looking, but *fewer* people actually reaching out.

On this data it's an artefact of how I generate enquiries, not a real signal. But it's exactly the shape you'd want to catch on real usage, and it's only visible because contacts sit next to the others rather than in a separate panel.

Where next — reorder what's below the top line, or add the seller/buyer concentration tiles?
