<a id="p59"></a>

## 59. Kobe — 2026-09-03 14:21

And after top-line, what should be the next components? Before actually visualizing the data, I want to confirm the overall structure of it


**Claude:**

Good instinct — worth settling before building six more panels.

Here's the structure I'd propose. The organising idea: **the dashboard should read as an argument, top to bottom**, and it should map onto the five research questions in `PROPOSAL.md` — so the same page serves the demo *and* the coursework.

## Proposed structure

| # | Section | Answers | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Top line** — activity over time, day/week/month | *How big is the moving-season effect?* | ✅ built |
| **2** | **Supply** — what's for sale | *What does a used dorm couch cost?* | partly |
| **3** | **Demand** — what people are looking for | — | partly |
| **4** | **Conversion** — does supply meet demand | — | partly |
| **5** | **Proximity & trust** — the product's actual thesis | *Trust circle size · which filter works · in-group discount* | partly |
| **6** | **Experiment** — what we tested, and the caveat | *Do match badges change behaviour?* | ✅ built |

### What goes in each

**2 · Supply** — category mix with sell-through and median price (built), price distribution by category and condition, **age of active inventory** (how much is stale), free items.

**3 · Demand** — top searches and the empty ones (built), filter usage, and the one I'd most want: **views by category against listings by category.** Where people look more than we stock is exactly where to recruit sellers.

**4 · Conversion** — the funnel (built), plus **days-to-sale by category and price band**, and conversion split by whether the buyer arrived via search or browse.

**5 · Proximity & trust** — sale distance (built), plus **inventory at each filter depth** (the trust-versus-selection curve, which is the most interesting chart in the proposal), which filter people drop first when the feed thins, contact rate by number of shared attributes, and in-group vs out-group sale price.

**6 · Experiment** — badge arms (built) with the planted-effects note.

### Why this order

It's a funnel in itself: *what happened* → *what we have* → *what people want* → *do those meet* → *does our thesis hold* → *what we actually tested*. Someone can stop reading after section 1 and still have the headline; someone reading to the end gets the argument.

```
def inventory_by_filter_depth(frames: dict[str, pd.DataFrame], sample_users: int = 200) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Every filter buys trust and costs inventory. This is that curve.

    For a sample of members, count how many active listings survive at each
    filter depth. The median row is the one to quote: it is what a typical
    member actually sees.
    """
    users, listings = frames["users"], frames["listings"]
    active = listings[listings["status"].isin(["active", "reserved"])]
    if users.empty or active.empty:
        return pd.DataFrame({"note": [EMPTY_NOTE]})
    sample = users.sample(min(sample_users, len(users)), random_state=0)

    rows = []
    for user in sample.itertuples():
        zip_ok = active["seller_zip"] == user.zip_code
        nat_ok = active["seller_nationality"] == user.nationality
        school_ok = active["seller_school"] == user.school
        rows.append(
            {
                "no_filters": len(active),
                "same_zip": int(zip_ok.sum()),
                "same_country": int(nat_ok.sum()),
                "same_school": int(school_ok.sum()),
                "zip_and_country": int((zip_ok & nat_ok).sum()),
                "all_three": int((zip_ok & nat_ok & school_ok).sum()),
            }
        )

    depth = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    return depth.describe().loc[["mean", "50%", "min", "max"]].round(1)

**Claude:**

Section 5 is built. **"Does the idea hold up?"** now sits below a heavy rule, with three claim panels and the badge experiment separated at the end as the one thing actually *tested*.

The trust-vs-selection curve reads well: amber bars mark where more than half of members fall below a usable feed, so the collapse is visible before you read a number. And the overlap chart greys out the 3-shared bar because only 435 impressions sit behind it — a handful of contacts either way swings that percentage, and the panel says so rather than letting it mislead.

## The finding worth putting in your report

The trust curve is **not planted** — it falls out of how the population is actually distributed:

| Filters on | Median feed | Members seeing <10 |
|---|---:|---:|
| None | 872 | 0% |
| Any one | ~113 | 0–26% |
| Any two | 5–11 | 49–63% |
| All three | **1** | **87%** |

One filter is survivable. **Two is where it breaks.** That's a direct answer to the proposal's *"how tight can a trust circle get before it stops working"*, it's genuinely emergent, and it justifies a real product decision — why the filters default to off.

The contact-rate panel also behaves: 2.19% → 2.67% → 2.96% across 0, 1 and 2 shared attributes, on tens of thousands of impressions each.

## Where this leaves the plan

| Section | Status |
|---|---|
| 1 Top line | ✅ day/week/month, 8 metrics |
| 2 Supply | Categories only — needs price-by-condition, stale inventory |
| 3 Demand | Searches only — needs views vs listings by category |
| 4 Conversion | Funnel only — needs days-to-sale |
| 5 Does the idea hold up? | ✅ three claims |
| 6 The one thing we tested | ✅ |

Two claims from our agreed list aren't built yet: *"Location and nationality matter; grade barely"* (which filters people actually use) and *"People discount for their own"* (in-group price).

## 62. Kobe — 2026-09-03 14:39

Wait i'm not so sure about what's for sale and what people are looking for represent supply, demand. What's your reasoning behind that?


**Claude:**

Fair challenge — and poking at it, the labels are leakier than I made them sound.

## Where the framing holds

**Supply is fine.** What's listed, in what categories, at what prices, how fresh — that's genuinely the seller side, and it's actionable in one direction: recruit more sellers, or different ones.

**Search is the cleanest demand signal we have.** Someone typing "office chair" is stating a want in their own words, unprompted, and it exists whether or not we have any. That's about as close to raw demand as this dataset gets.

## Where it doesn't

**Views aren't really demand.** A view happens because someone *looked* at something we *chose to show them*. If the feed is 30% furniture, furniture gets viewed a lot — that's our ranking, not their preference. So views are demand filtered through supply, and calling them demand overstates it.

**Sell-through is in the wrong section.** I put it under Supply, but sold ÷ listed is precisely supply meeting demand. It belongs in Conversion.

**Stale inventory is ambiguous.** Old listings could mean too much supply *or* too little demand. It reads as a supply-health number but doesn't isolate a cause.

## What I actually think

The supply/demand framing only earns its keep if we use it for **one specific thing: the mismatch.** Where people search or look more than we stock — that's the chart that justifies the whole vocabulary, and it's directly actionable ("go recruit textbook sellers"). Two parallel lists of charts labelled Supply and Demand, without that comparison, is economics vocabulary doing no work.

Three ways to go:

Move sell-through to Conversion. The centrepiece becomes the gap by category - where demand outruns stock. The vocabulary then earns itself."
        },
        {
          "label": "Drop the economics, use plain labels",
          "description": "\"What's listed\" / \"What people look for\" / \"What happens\". Makes no claim the data cannot support, and nobody has to agree with your definition of demand. Loses the framing that makes the mismatch chart feel like a conclusion rather than a chart."
        },
        {

        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

**Claude:**

Before building the mismatch chart, I have to flag something — **the data can't currently support it**, and it would produce a chart that looks meaningful and isn't.

There are three possible demand-by-category signals, and all three fail:

| Signal | Counts | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| Category filter toggles | clothing 56, kitchen 54, furniture 52, textbooks 51… | My generator picks the category with `rng.choice(CATEGORIES)` — **uniform**. Flat by construction. |
| Search queries | vacuum 99, rice cooker 93, desk 87, headphones 87… | Same problem: terms are drawn uniformly from a hand-written list. Also flat. |
| Views by category | Tracks listings closely | Supply-driven — we showed them furniture because we stock furniture. |

So a supply-vs-demand gap chart today would show either **noise around a flat line**, or **supply plotted against itself**. Either way it would invite a conclusion the data can't carry — which is exactly the failure mode we'd be building the section to avoid.

## The fix is small and belongs in the generator

Give categories a **demand distribution distinct from their supply distribution**. Concretely: weight the search terms and category filter toggles so that, say, textbooks and electronics are wanted more than they're stocked, and furniture is stocked more than it's wanted.

That's the same class of thing as the May/August seasonality — scenery, not one of the research questions — so it goes in the planted-effects table in `data_visualization_spec.md` §6 and nobody can mistake it for a discovery.

It also makes the mismatch chart genuinely *do* something: it would show a real gap, computed honestly from two independent signals, and the "recruit textbook sellers" conclusion would follow from the numbers rather than from me writing it in a caption.

Two things I'd want your call on:

**1. Should I add demand weights to the generator?** It means regenerating and reseeding again (one command each), and it's the only way the Demand section says anything.

**2. If yes — which way round?** I'd suggest demand skewing toward textbooks, electronics and kitchen (things students need on arrival), while supply skews to furniture (what people dump at move-out). That's a plausible real-world story for this marketplace and makes the seasonal and category views tell a consistent one.

If you'd rather not touch the generator again, the honest alternative is to drop the mismatch chart and let Demand be searches only — in which case the supply/demand framing goes back to being labels rather than an argument, and plain names would be better.

**One thing worth knowing: §3 still carries real weight**, just not the weight I originally claimed. Search *volume* is uniform by construction, so "vacuum is more wanted than desks" means nothing. But whether a search **returns anything** is computed by matching real queries against real titles — so this is genuine:

```
textbook       82 searches   82 empty
office chair   79 searches   79 empty
vacuum         99 searches    0 empty

Nobody set that. It says the catalogue has plenty of textbooks and chairs, but their titles never contain the words people would search for — *"Corporate Finance (Berk) 5th ed."*, *"HON Ignition, size C"*. That's a real, fixable product problem, and it's the honest headline for that section: not *what* people want, but *what we fail to surface when they ask*.

I'll frame the panel as "Searches that find nothing" rather than "Demand", and let it point at the searchability gap.

Shall I build §2–§4 on that basis?

## What the new panels surfaced

**Two real problems, neither of which I planted:**

**68% of live inventory is over three months old.** 596 of 872 listings. The feed looks well-stocked and mostly isn't — those items are being scrolled past. That's a genuine consequence of the sell-through rate combined with nothing ever expiring.

**"Searches that find nothing" is a genuine bug, not missing stock.** `textbook` 82, `office chair` 79, `bookshelf` 76, `ikea desk` 75 — we *have* all of those. Search matches on title only, and the titles say "Corporate Finance (Berk) 5th ed." and "HON Ignition, size C". The catalogue is there and unreachable. That's a fixable backend change: match category and subcategory too.

Also note `cat` (59) and `apartment` (57) legitimately return nothing — pets and housing are out of scope. Those are correct empties, which makes the panel more honest than a flat "we're missing stock" reading.

**One clean number for the report:** a new item asks **112% more** than a used—fair one — real pricing guidance for the posting form, straight from the price ladder.

**Claude:**

You're right, and I oversold it. That curve mostly restates something mechanical — *filter the feed, see fewer things* — and dressing it up as a finding was a stretch. It's really a **UX fact** ("this is why filters default to off"), not evidence that shared affiliation does anything.

So: I'll move it out of the claims section into the operator half where it belongs, and build the commonality claim properly. Right now that claim rests on one chart, and there's much stronger evidence available.

The strongest test I can build asks: **among the people who actually saw a listing, did the one who bought it share more with the seller than the average viewer did?**

That's better than contact rate because it controls for exposure. If people in 10027 see more 10027 listings, of course they contact more of them — that's proximity, not trust. But if, *among the same pool of viewers*, buyers consistently share more with sellers than non-buyers, that's the thesis doing work.

**Claude:**

Restructured. The claim now stands on **two panels that answer different halves of the question**, side by side.

**Left — do people reach out more?** Yes: 2.19% → 2.67% → 2.96% as shared attributes go 0 → 1 → 2, on tens of thousands of impressions each.

**Right — do they actually buy more?** No. Among people who saw the *same* listing, the buyer shared 0.619 of three attributes against 0.604 for everyone else. Same school is identical at 12.5%; buyers were even slightly *less* likely to share a country.

That contrast is the interesting part, and it's stronger than either chart alone:

> **Having something in common makes people reach out — but among people considering the same item, it doesn't decide who goes through with it.**

Methodologically the right-hand panel is the better test, which is worth saying in your report. "Buyers share a lot with sellers" would be a meaningless statistic — people near a seller see more of their listings to begin with, so overlap would look high from proximity alone. Holding the *listing* constant and comparing the buyer against the other viewers cancels exposure out. What's left is whether affiliation predicted the outcome, and here it didn't.

The filter curve moved to the operator half, retitled **"Why the trust filters default to off"** — which is honestly what it shows: a product decision justified by data, not a finding about behaviour.

Two claims from our list are still unbuilt: *"Location and nationality matter; grade barely"* and *"People discount for their own."* Given how the buyer-vs-viewer result turned out, the in-group discount one may be worth doing next — it tests the same thesis on price rather than on who buys.

## 66. Kobe — 2026-09-03 16:03

what does your 'The one thing we tested' prove? can you explain it to me in layperson term?


**Claude:**

Good question — it's doing something genuinely different from every other panel, and that difference is the point.

## Why it's not like the other charts

Every other panel **observes** what happened. That's useful but limited, because you can never fully separate cause from coincidence.

Take "people trade with people near them." You see lots of same-ZIP sales — but is that because proximity builds trust, or just because the feed shows you nearby stuff, so you had more chances to buy it? You genuinely can't tell from the chart.

This one is different: **we flipped a coin.**

## What we actually did

Every time a listing was shown to someone, a coin decided whether the match badges appeared. Heads, they saw "SAME ZIP · SAME SCHOOL." Tails, they saw the same listing with nothing.

```
No badges shown    28,760 times    637 people got in touch    2.21%
Badges shown       28,804 times    777 people got in touch    2.70%
```

Because the coin decided — not the person, not the item, not the location — the two groups are otherwise identical. Same listings, same prices, same distances, same mix of people. **The only difference is the badge.**

So if one group behaves differently, the badge caused it. That's the whole logic, and it's the same reason drug trials give half the patients a sugar pill.

Here, people who saw badges reached out about **22% more often**.

## What it proves, honestly

On real users, that would be strong evidence the badges do their job — the single most useful thing this product could learn.

On the data we have, it proves something narrower: **the measurement works.** I built the fake data with a badge effect deliberately included, and the analysis correctly found it. So the plumbing is right — the coin flip is recorded, the two groups are compared properly, the maths is sound. Point it at real usage and it would give you a real answer.

That's still worth having on the page, and worth saying plainly in the report: *"we built and validated the experiment; here's what it will measure once people use the product."*

The panel already carries that caveat in the grey box underneath, precisely so nobody reads the 22% as a fact about Columbia students.

<a id="p67"></a>

## 67. Kobe — 2026-09-03 16:05

when i present the result to the group, tell me how can i explain this in easy way. Write a simple script for me


**Claude:**

Here's a script — roughly 90 seconds spoken. Written the way you'd actually say it, not the way it'd be written down.

---

**[Pull up the dashboard, scroll to "The one thing we tested"]**

> "So everything above this line is us *watching* what happened. This last bit is different — this is the one thing we actually **tested**.
>
> Here's the problem with just watching. If I show you a chart saying people mostly buy from sellers nearby, that sounds like proximity builds trust. But it might just be that the app shows you nearby stuff, so of course you buy it. You can't tell which. Same story with the school and country badges — maybe they work, maybe people who share a school just bump into each other's listings more.
>
> So we did the thing drug trials do. Every time someone was shown an item, **a coin flip decided whether the match badges appeared.** Heads, you see 'SAME ZIP, SAME SCHOOL.' Tails, you see the exact same item with nothing on it.
>
> **[point at the two boxes]**
>
> That's about 29,000 times each. Same listings, same prices, same people — the *only* difference is whether the badge showed up.
>
> Without badges, 2.2% of people contacted the seller. With badges, 2.7%. That's about **22% more people reaching out.**
>
> And because the coin decided, not the person, that difference has to be the badge. Nothing else was different.
>
> Now — the honest part. Our data is generated, so I built that effect in on purpose. What this proves today isn't 'badges work on Columbia students.' It proves **the experiment itself works** — the coin flip gets recorded, the two groups get compared properly, the maths is right. It found the effect it was supposed to find.
>
> Which means the day we have real users, this exact page answers our most important question with no extra work. That's the bit I'd put in the report."

---

**If you only get 20 seconds**, cut to this:

> "Everything else on this page is us watching what happened, which can't prove cause. This one's a real experiment — a coin flip decided who saw match badges, so the two groups are identical apart from that. Badges got 22% more people contacting sellers. On our fake data that proves the measurement works; point it at real users and it answers whether the whole idea is right."

---

Two tips for delivering it:

**Lead with the problem, not the method.** "Here's why charts can't prove cause" earns you thirty seconds of attention. "We ran an A/B test" loses the room.

**Say the caveat yourself, early and calmly.** If someone else raises it first it sounds like you got caught; if you raise it, it sounds like you understand your own work. And "the experiment is built and validated, ready for real users" is genuinely a good result to be reporting.

**Claude:**

**No.** The dashboard is marketplace-wide, not personalised.

`current_user` appears only to require you to be signed in — the signed-in person's ZIP is never used in any query. Every "viewer" you see in that grep is a *row* in `listing_views`, not you.

So Brian in 10027 and someone in Park Slope see **identical numbers**.

That's the opposite of the feed, which is entirely built around your ZIP and radius. Deliberate, and I think right for an operator dashboard — "how is the marketplace doing" shouldn't change depending on who asks.

**Location does appear in the data, just not as a filter:**

- *How far a sold item travelled* — buyer's ZIP to the listing's ZIP, across all sales
- *Why the trust filters default to off* — samples 300 members and computes what each would see, so it's an average over the whole membership, not your feed
- *Contact rate by shared attributes* — includes same-ZIP as one of the three

If you'd rather it *were* location-aware, there are two quite different versions:

**"My neighbourhood"** — filter everything to listings and members in your ZIP or radius. Makes it a personal view: how's the market where I actually shop. Every endpoint needs the viewer's ZIP, and the small-ZIP numbers get noisy fast.

**Geography as its own panel** — keep the dashboard global, but add a breakdown *by* ZIP or borough: where listings concentrate, where sales happen, which neighbourhoods are supply-heavy versus demand-heavy. No filtering, just location as a dimension. Cheaper, and probably more interesting for a group presentation than "here's my street."

I'd lean toward the second if you want location in there. Want me to add it?

**Claude:**

Good — numbers are **stable** across repeated loads. So it's not random wobble. You were seeing a real effect, and my earlier answer was wrong.

## What's actually happening

The dashboard doesn't *filter* by your location. But **you are one of the 1,000 members in the data**, so changing your ZIP edits a row that the aggregates read.

Measured directly, moving `@brian_dw` from 10027 to Park Slope:

| Metric | 10027 | 11215 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Listings, sold, views | 1,350 / 452 / 64,236 | **unchanged** |
| Sales in same-ZIP band | 102 | **unchanged** |
| Trust curve, "Same ZIP" | 149 | **125** |
| Contact rate, 0 shared | 2.177% | 2.191% |

Two of those move, for two different reasons:

**The trust curve moves a lot** because it samples 300 members and asks "what would this person see with same-ZIP on?" You're in that sample. 10027 is the densest ZIP in the corpus, so *your* answer is large; Park Slope's is small — and with only 300 people sampled, swapping one from the top of the distribution shifts the median several points.

**The overlap panels move slightly** because your ZIP is compared against sellers' ZIPs across every impression you've ever had. Change your ZIP and thousands of view rows get reclassified from "shared" to "not shared."

Everything that doesn't involve *you* — total listings, sales, views, sale distances — is rock solid.

## Two things worth fixing

**The trust curve is too twitchy.** One member out of 300 shouldn't move the median by 24. Raising the sample to all 1,000 members would make it stable and cost almost nothing — it's a vectorised operation over 872 listings.

**Also: I had your ZIP wrong.** The sign-in reported `@brian_dw, ZIP 10025` — you'd already changed it in the UI, and I've been saying 10027 all along. My test restored it to 10027 at the end, so if you'd set 10025 deliberately, change it back.

Want me to bump the trust-curve sample so that panel stops reacting to a single person?

**Claude:**

Because **all 82 searches for "textbook" returned zero results** — there was nothing to click.

Not a bug in the click tracking. A bug in search:

```
"textbook"   82 searches → 0 results → 0 clicks
we have      272 listings in the textbooks category
titles say   "Epidemiology — full course bundle"
             "Marketing Strategy 9th ed. + solutions manual"
             "Linear Algebra (McGraw-Hill), international edition"
listings whose title contains the word "textbook":  0
```

Compare with one that works: `"vacuum"` → 99 searches, **36 clicks**, because 19 titles actually contain the word "vacuum".

## The cause

Search matches on **title only**. Nobody writes "textbook" in a listing title — they write the course name. Same for `office chair` (79 empty; ours say "HON Ignition, size C") and `bookshelf` (76 empty; ours say "IKEA KALLAX shelf unit, oak").

So a third of all searches fail while the inventory sits right there. From the seller's side it's invisible: your listing is live, it just can't be found by the word a buyer would use.

## The fix is small

Search currently does:

```python
Listing.title.ilike(like) | Listing.description.ilike(like)
```

Add category and subcategory to that, and `"textbook"` immediately matches all 272 — because the category *is* `textbooks`. Same for `office chair` → the `chairs` subcategory, `bookshelf` → `storage_shelving`.

That's a genuine product improvement found by the dashboard, which is a decent thing to be able to say in the presentation: *"we built the dashboard, and it immediately showed us a third of searches were failing on stock we already had."*

It's a change to `services/feed.py`, which is Jae and Vinayak's file. Want me to make it, or write it up for them?

Two smaller notes while you're in that panel: `cat` (59) and `apartment` (57) also return nothing, and those are **correct** — pets and housing are deliberately out of scope, housing for fair-housing reasons. So not every empty search is a failure. And the numbers behind these are uniform by construction, so read them as *which* searches fail, never as *how much* people want a thing.

```
LOWLIGHTS — working with Claude Code on Columbia Market
Kobe · ENGI 4503 · week of 3 September 2026

I owned the data component: the seeded corpus, the behavioural data, and the
dashboard. Most of it went well. These are the parts that didn't.

1. It answered from the code instead of from the running system.
I asked whether the dashboard was location-based. It said no — the aggregates
are marketplace-wide and the signed-in user's ZIP is never used. I believed it,
because it had just read the file. Then I changed my ZIP in the header and
watched numbers move. When I pushed back, it ran an actual before-and-after
test and found two panels do change: the trust-filter curve went from 149 to
125, because I am one of the 300 members it samples. What went wrong is that it
reasoned from function signatures — "no viewer parameter, therefore not
personalised" — which was true about the code and false about the behaviour. I
now ask it to prove claims by running something rather than by reading.

2. It fixed two symptoms before finding the cause.
Listing images showed as broken. It generated the missing image files. Still
broken. It changed how the page falls back. Still broken. Only on the third
pass did it check whether the database and the CSV files agreed — and they
didn't. I had regenerated the data, which produced new listing IDs, without
reloading the database, so 17 of the 24 listings on screen pointed at files
that no longer existed. Each fix was locally correct and none of them addressed
the problem. When a fix doesn't work, the next move is to re-diagnose, not to
try another fix.

3. It proposed an analysis the data could not support.
We agreed a "supply versus demand" section whose centrepiece would show
categories where people want more than we stock. It began building before
checking whether the data had a demand signal at all. It didn't: the generator
picks search terms and category filters uniformly at random, so both signals
are flat by construction and the chart would have shown noise dressed as
insight. It caught this itself, but only once it started writing the query —
after I had approved the structure on the strength of the description.

4. It oversold a result and I nearly accepted it.
It called the trust-filter curve "the most interesting chart in the proposal."
Looking at it properly, the chart mostly says that if you filter a list you get
a shorter list. That is mechanical, not a finding. I said so and it agreed
immediately, then moved the panel out of the findings section into the product
section where it works as a justification for a default setting. The lesson
isn't that it lied. It's that confident framing is cheap, and my job is to ask
what a chart would look like if it were trivially true.

5. It verified the wrong layer and declared something working.
I told it sign-in didn't work. It had already "verified" sign-in by calling the
API directly, which worked fine. The bug was in the page: a second attempt
within sixty seconds returns sent:false, meaning a link was already sent, and
the page treated that as failure and rendered nothing — no error, no countdown,
a dead button. Testing the API proved the API worked. It proved nothing about
what a person sees.

The pattern
Four of these five were caught by me looking at the screen, not by the agent
checking its own work. It is fluent enough that its explanations sound like
verification when they aren't, and it is fast and usually right, which is
exactly what makes the failures quiet. The habit I've built is to separate the
two: I ask "what did you run to check that?" and treat anything else as a
hypothesis.
```

"""Convert a Claude Code session transcript (.jsonl) into a readable Markdown document.

The raw log is a line-per-event stream that mixes conversation turns with a lot of
housekeeping: mode switches, token reminders, file-history snapshots, and base64
screenshots. This keeps the conversation and drops the rest.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import datetime as dt
import json
import re
import sys

# Event kinds that carry no conversation -- session bookkeeping only.
SKIP_TYPES = {
    "mode", "permission-mode", "atis-latch", "bridge-session", "ai-title",
    "last-prompt", "frame-link", "pr-link", "file-history-snapshot",
    "file-history-delta", "queue-operation", "artifact-comment-monitor",
    "artifact-autoreact-ledger", "attachment", "system",
}

TOOL_INPUT_LIMIT = 2500
TOOL_RESULT_LIMIT = 2500
THINKING_LIMIT = 6000

# System-injected blocks that arrive inside user messages but were never typed.
REMINDER_RE = re.compile(r"<system-reminder>.*?</system-reminder>", re.DOTALL)
B64_RE = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9+/]{200,}={0,2}")


def clean(text: str) -> str:
    text = REMINDER_RE.sub("", text)
    text = B64_RE.sub("[binary data omitted]", text)
    return text.strip()


def clip(text: str, limit: int) -> str:
    if len(text) <= limit:
        return text
    kept = text[:limit].rstrip()
    return "%s\n… [%s more characters]" % (kept, format(len(text) - limit, ","))


def fence(text: str, lang: str = "") -> str:
    """Fence a block, widening the fence if the body contains one of its own."""
    ticks = "```"
    while ticks in text:
        ticks += "`"
    return "%s%s\n%s\n%s" % (ticks, lang, text, ticks)


def flatten(content) -> str:
    """Tool results arrive as a string, or as a list of text/image blocks."""
    if isinstance(content, str):
        return content
    if isinstance(content, list):
        parts = []
        for block in content:
            if not isinstance(block, dict):
                parts.append(str(block))
            elif block.get("type") == "text":
                parts.append(block.get("text", ""))
            elif block.get("type") == "image":
                parts.append("[image]")
            else:
                parts.append("[%s]" % block.get("type"))
        return "\n".join(parts)
    return "" if content is None else
